nagaland: Nagaland lies in the north-eastern region of India and is bordered by Arunachal Pradesh to the north, Assam to the west, Manipur to the south and the Naga Self-Administered Zone of the Sagaing Region of Myanmar to the east. It is a mountainous state of 16,579 square kilometres. It consists of 17 administrative districts and is inhabited by 17 major tribes, each distinct in customs, language and dress. The origin of the word Naga is unclear.

The early history of the Nagas is unclear. Ethnic groups migrated at different times and established their own mountain territories and village states. The first Europeans to enter the Naga Hills were Captain Francis Jenkins and Lieutenant Robert Pemberton in 1832. The British recorded ten military expeditions between 1839 and 1850 to stop raids on tea estates and trading posts. At the Battle of Kikrüma in February 1851 people died on both sides, after which the British adopted a policy of non-interference.

In 1944 the Japanese Army, with the Indian National Army, invaded from Burma and tried to take India through Kohima. The battle was fought from 4 April to 22 June 1944, coordinated with action at Imphal, and British and Indian troops repelled the attackers. After Indian independence the Naga National Council under Zapu Phizo demanded an independent Naga state and began an armed insurgency, and the Indian Army was sent in 1955. The State of Nagaland was formally inaugurated on 1 December 1963 as the 16th state of the Indian Union.

Nagaland had a population of 1,980,602 at the 2011 census. Kohima is the capital. The Naga people form over 90 percent of the population and speak mostly Sino-Tibetan languages. English is the official language and the medium of education, and Nagamese, a creole based on Assamese, is widely spoken. At the 2011 census 87.93 percent of residents were Christian, and Nagaland is known as the most Baptist state in the world.
nagasaki: The first recorded contact between Portuguese explorers and Japan came in 1543. In 1569 the daimyō Ōmura Sumitada granted a permit for a port for Portuguese ships at Nagasaki, set up in 1571 under the Jesuit missionary Gaspar Vilela. The harbour village grew into a diverse port city, and Portuguese imports such as tobacco and the sponge-cake castellas entered Japanese culture. In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi placed it under his direct control and ordered the missionaries expelled, an order largely unenforced.

On Hideyoshi's order, twenty-six Catholics were crucified at Nagasaki in the following decade. Catholicism was officially banned in 1614, and a brutal persecution followed in which thousands of converts were killed, tortured or forced to renounce their faith. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 the Portuguese were expelled, and the Dutch were moved from Hirado to Dejima, the artificial island in Nagasaki harbour that had been the Portuguese trading post. In 1720 the ban on Dutch books was lifted, and scholars flocked to Nagasaki to study European science and art, a movement called rangaku. Nagasaki became a treaty port in 1859 and later a centre of shipbuilding under Mitsubishi.

On 9 August 1945 the Boeing B-29 Bockscar, commanded by Major Charles Sweeney, carried a plutonium bomb called Fat Man from Tinian. Its primary target was Kokura, which was hidden by cloud and smoke, so it flew to the secondary target, Nagasaki, where cloud again obscured the city. A gap in the cloud let the crew see a racetrack, and they dropped the bomb on the Urakami Valley, between the Mitsubishi Steel and Arms Works and the Mitsubishi-Urakami Ordnance Works. It exploded at 11:02 a.m. at about 1,800 feet. The dead numbered 35,000, including 150 Japanese soldiers, 6,200 of the 7,500 employees of the Mitsubishi Munitions plant and 24,000 others, among them 2,000 Koreans.

Nagasaki is the capital and largest city of Nagasaki Prefecture, on Kyushu, and lies at the head of a long bay that forms the best natural harbour on the island. The city was rebuilt after the war, with new churches and temples, and a museum and memorials to the bombing; it remains primarily a port city with a shipbuilding industry. The Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
nagoya: Nagoya lies on the Pacific coast of central Honshu, north of Ise Bay on the Nōbi Plain, one of the most fertile areas of Japan. The city was built on low plateaus to keep off floodwaters. The Kiso River runs along its western border, and the Shōnai River comes from the northeast and turns south towards the bay. The orderly grid of its streets is ultimately credited to the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu.

Oda Nobunaga and his protégés Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu were warlords based in the Nagoya area who gradually unified Japan. In 1610 Ieyasu moved the capital of Owari Province from Kiyosu, about seven kilometres away, to a more strategic site in what is now Nagoya. Nagoya Castle was built partly from materials taken from Kiyosu Castle, and the whole town around it, some 60,000 people, moved with it. Nearby Atsuta Shrine became a waystation called Miya on the Tōkaidō road between Kyoto and Edo, and a town grew up to serve travellers. The castle town and the shrine town together formed the city.

Nagoya was a major trading city and the seat of the Owari lords, the most important house of the Tokugawa clan. They encouraged trade and the arts, above all Tokugawa Muneharu, the seventh lord, who took a keen interest in drama and lived lavishly; actors began to visit the city, and wealthy merchants supported the arts further. Nō and Kyōgen theatre date back to the Owari lords, and the Misono-za, one of Japan's grand kabuki stages, developed in the Edo period.

In the early 1900s a convergence of economic factors brought rapid growth. The area's automobile, aviation and shipbuilding industries flourished, following older crafts such as bicycles, sewing machines and timepieces, and then ceramics, chemicals, oil, petrochemicals and steel. These industries made Nagoya a target of American air raids in the Pacific War, when the Mitsubishi A6M Zero fighter was built there, and many old buildings and artefacts were destroyed. The city had 153,370 households at the war's end in 1945, and it rebuilt as a leading centre of industry.

Nagoya is the capital of Aichi Prefecture and the largest city of the Chūbu region, with about 2.3 million people. It is the principal city of the Chūkyō metropolitan area, and its seaport is the largest in Japan. It is linked to Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto by the Tōkaidō Shinkansen. Atsuta Shrine and Nagoya Castle are its two best-known sights, and UNESCO recognises it as a Design City.
namibia: Namibia covers 825,615 square kilometres and is the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa. It borders the Atlantic Ocean, Angola, Zambia through the Caprivi Strip, Botswana and South Africa. Its landscape falls into five areas: the Central Plateau, the Namib Desert, the Great Escarpment, the Bushveld and the Kalahari Desert. The Namib, a hyper-arid expanse of gravel plains and dunes, runs along the whole coast and gives the country its name; Namib is a Khoi word meaning vast place. The Central Plateau holds the highest point, Königstein, at 2,573 metres.

The Khoikhoi as pastoralists and the San as hunter-gatherers lived in the dry lands for thousands of years, and Damara and Nama peoples also inhabited them. Around the 14th century Bantu peoples began to arrive, and from 1600 the Owambo formed kingdoms such as Ondonga and Oukwanyama. The Portuguese navigators Diogo Cão in 1485 and Bartolomeu Dias in 1486 were the first Europeans to land, but did not claim the area. From the late 18th century the Oorlam people crossed the Orange River from the Dutch Cape Colony, and conflict with the Herero led to the Nama-Herero War of 1880.

In 1878 the Cape Colony annexed Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands, and in 1884 the German Empire established rule over most of the territory as German South West Africa. Between 1904–08 German troops waged a punitive campaign against the Herero and Nama that escalated into what is often called the first genocide of the 20th century. South African forces defeated the Germans in 1915, and the League of Nations mandated the colony to South Africa in 1920.

South Africa applied apartheid to the territory after the National Party won power in 1948. The United Nations assumed direct responsibility in 1966, though South Africa kept de facto rule until 1973, when the UN recognised SWAPO as the official representative of the Namibian people. Namibia became independent in March 1990 after the South African Border War, and Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands stayed under South African control until 1994. Namibia is a parliamentary democracy, and the 2023 census counted 3,022,401 people.
nanjing: Nanjing lies in the Yangtze River Delta, in the lower Yangtze drainage area, in the southwestern corner of Jiangsu province. The Yangtze flows past the west side and then the north side of the city, and the Ningzheng Ridge surrounds it to the north, east and south. The Qinhuai River, called the mother river of Nanjing, runs through the main urban area to join the Yangtze, and Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake lie within the city. The climate is humid subtropical, shaped by the East Asian monsoon, with very hot summers.

Human habitation in the area dates to the Neolithic period. A settlement called Jinling existed around the 4th century BCE, and after Qin's unification it was renamed Moling. Throughout the Six Dynasties period the regimes of the southeast kept their administrative centre at Jiankang, originally Jianye, with brief exceptions in 221–229, 265–267 and 552–554. The city was the capital of Eastern Wu from 229 to 280, of the Eastern Jin and of each of the Southern dynasties, which ruled southern China from 317 to 589.

Emperor Wen of Sui ordered Jiankang demolished in 589, levelling its walls, palaces and residences and deporting the Chen ruler and officials to the Sui capital. For three centuries the settlement was demoted. It was the capital of the Southern Tang from 937 to 975. In 1356 Zhu Yuanzhang captured the area and reorganised it as Yingtian Prefecture; in 1368 he took the throne there as the Hongwu Emperor, founding the Ming dynasty, and named it Nanjing, Southern Capital. It was the Ming capital until 1421.

The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom held it from 1853 to 1864. After the Xinhai Revolution, delegates elected Sun Yat-sen provisional president there on 29 December 1911, and he was sworn in on 1 January 1912. Nanjing was the capital of the Republic of China from 1927 to 1937 and again from 1946 to 1949, and under Japanese occupation the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist regime from 1940 to 1945. It suffered atrocities, most notably the Nanjing Massacre of 1937–1938. Communist forces captured it in April 1949, and it became capital of Jiangsu in 1952.

Nanjing is the capital of Jiangsu province and one of the Four Great Ancient Capitals of China. Its heritage sites include the Presidential Palace, the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum, the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum and the city wall. The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, a road and rail bridge begun in 1960 and opened to traffic in 1968, was designed and built by Chinese engineers.
nantes: Nantes lies in north-western France on the Loire, 50 kilometres from the Atlantic coast and 340 kilometres south-west of Paris. With the seaport of Saint-Nazaire on the Loire estuary it forms one of the main north-western agglomerations of France, and it is the seat of the Loire-Atlantique department and of the Pays de la Loire region. The city belongs historically and culturally to Brittany, and its omission from the modern administrative region of Brittany is controversial.

The first inhabitants settled in the Bronze Age, apparently drawn by small iron and tin deposits, and the area exported tin as far as Ireland. Nantes remained allied with the Roman Empire until its collapse in the fifth century. Around 490 the Franks under Clovis I took it from the Visigoths after a sixty-day siege. It was the seat of a bishopric at the end of the Roman era and was captured by the Bretons in 851.

The marriage of Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII of France in 1491 began the union of the duchy with the French crown, ratified in 1532. Rennes then became the provincial capital, while Nantes kept a financial role through its Chamber of Accounts. In the 17th century it gradually became the largest port in France and was responsible for nearly half of the 18th-century French Atlantic slave trade.

On 18 July 1789 locals seized the Castle of the Dukes of Brittany in imitation of the storming of the Bastille. The slave trade, outlawed by the Revolution, re-established itself in the first decades of the 19th century, and Nantes was the last French port to conduct it, until about 1827. About 400,000 people may have been deported to the colonies.

Nantes has 327,734 inhabitants in the city proper and 1,050,815 in the metropolitan area, making it the sixth-largest city in France. It has 127 buildings listed as monuments historiques. Along the Loire, a memorial to slavery has a path of 2,000 glass inserts, 1,710 of them naming slave ships and their dates of departure from Nantes.
naples: The city lies on the Gulf of Naples, on the western coast of southern Italy, and rises from sea level to an elevation of 450 metres. It stands between two volcanic regions, Mount Vesuvius and the Phlegraean Fields. The islands of Procida, Capri and Ischia can be reached from Naples by hydrofoil and ferry, and Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast lie to the south. Nearby are the Roman ruins of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis and Stabiae, destroyed in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, and to the west the port towns of Pozzuoli and Baia, part of the Roman naval facility of Portus Julius.

The site has been inhabited since the Neolithic period. In the second millennium BCE a Mycenaean settlement arose not far from the future city. Sailors from the Greek island of Rhodes probably established a small commercial port called Parthenope, named for a Siren of Greek mythology, on the island of Megaride in the ninth century BCE. By the eighth century BCE Cumaeans had expanded it to include Monte Echia, and in the sixth century BCE it was refounded as Neápolis, becoming one of the foremost cities of Magna Graecia.

The city grew rapidly under the influence of the Greek city-state of Syracuse and became an ally of the Roman Republic against Carthage. During the Samnite Wars it was captured by the Samnites, but the Romans soon took it from them and made it a Roman colony. In the Punic Wars its strong walls repelled the Carthaginian general Hannibal. Naples was later the capital of the Duchy of Naples (661–1139), of the Kingdom of Naples (1282–1816) and of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until the unification of Italy in 1861.

Between 1925 and 1936 the Fascist regime expanded and upgraded the city. In the later years of the Second World War it suffered severe damage from the bombing of the Allied forces. The Four Days of Naples, an uprising against the German occupation forces, lasted from 27 to 30 September 1943, just before Allied forces arrived on 1 October. The city was extensively rebuilt after the war.

Naples is the capital of the region of Campania and the largest city of southern Italy, with 905,050 residents within its administrative boundaries. Its historic centre was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1995. The University of Naples Federico II, founded by Frederick II in 1224, is thought to be the oldest state university in the world. Caravaggio's arrival in 1606 was a critical factor in the development of the Neapolitan school of painting, and the Teatro di San Carlo opera house dates from the 18th century.
napoleon: Napoleon Bonaparte was born Napoleone di Buonaparte on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, a year after the Republic of Genoa ceded the island to France. His family was of Italian origin, the Buonapartes descending from a minor Tuscan noble family that had moved to Corsica in the 16th century. With the support of the French governor Charles Louis de Marbeuf, his father's patron, he obtained a royal bursary to a military academy on the mainland, and in September 1785 he was commissioned a second lieutenant in the artillery. He supported the French Revolution, but after a failed attempt to take Ajaccio in June 1793 the family fled to Toulon.

Napoleon rose rapidly after winning the siege of Toulon in 1793, and in 1796 a campaign against the Austrians and their Italian allies made him a national hero. In 1798 he led an invasion of Egypt and Syria. On 9 November 1799 (18 Brumaire) he and his fellow conspirators launched a coup against the Directory, and he became First Consul. He won the Battle of Marengo in 1800, sold Louisiana to the United States in 1803 and crowned himself Emperor of the French in December 1804.

He defeated the Third Coalition at Austerlitz, which led to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and beat Prussia in 1806 and Russia in 1807. In 1808 he installed his brother Joseph as King of Spain, provoking the Peninsular War. His invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in a catastrophic winter retreat from Moscow. After defeat at Leipzig in 1813 he abdicated in April 1814 and was exiled to Elba. He escaped ten months later, but the Seventh Coalition defeated him at Waterloo in June 1815.

The British sent him to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died on 5 May 1821 of stomach cancer, aged 51. His reforms included the Napoleonic Code, a system of public education, the Banque de France and the Concordat of 1801 with the Catholic Church, and he gave civil and religious equality to Protestants and Jews. Against this stand wars that historians say cost six million lives, the plunder of conquered territories, the abolition of the free press and of directly elected representative government, and the reinstatement of slavery in French colonies. Historians still debate whether he was an enlightened despot who laid the foundations of modern Europe or a man who brought great misery.
nationalism: Scholars frequently place the beginning of nationalism in the late 18th or early 19th century, with the American Declaration of Independence or the French Revolution, though there is ongoing debate about forms of it in the Middle Ages and even antiquity. The French Revolution of 1789 is seen as an important starting point, above all for its impact on Germans, Italians and European intellectuals. The template of mobilising public opinion around a new state based on popular sovereignty went back further, to earlier constitutionalist movements such as the Corsican Republic and the American Revolution.

Primordialism, which arose in the Romantic era, held that there have always been nations, and most scholars have rejected it. Modernist accounts argue that nationalism arises in societies with a self-sustaining industrial economy, a central authority and a shared language. Benedict Anderson tied it to print capitalism and printed media in vernacular languages, and described nations as socially constructed communities imagined by those who belong to them.

Nationalism holds that the nation should be congruent with the state, that it should govern itself free from outside interference, and that it is the only rightful source of political power. It aims to build a single national identity from shared characteristics such as culture, ethnicity, homeland, language, religion or a belief in a shared history.

The most common classification is civic or ethnic, a distinction popularised in the 1950s by Hans Kohn and criticised since the 1980s as too rigid. Civic nationalism defines the nation as an association of people with equal political rights; Ernest Renan in 1882 called the nation a daily referendum. Ethnic nationalism defines it by shared heritage, language, faith and ancestry. Creole nationalism arose among the descendants of colonisers in Latin America after Napoleon seized control of Spain and Portugal, and independence was won in civil wars between 1808 and 1826.

In the 19th century nationalism became one of the most significant political and social forces in history, and it is typically listed among the top causes of the First World War. Napoleon's conquests of the German and Italian states around 1800 to 1806 stimulated demands for national unity. Japan's defeat of Russia in 1905 spurred new interest in nationalism in China, Turkey and Persia, and in China Sun Yat-sen founded the Kuomintang in defiance of the declining empire. Nationalism has been a feature of movements for freedom and justice, and has also been used to legitimise racial, ethnic and religious divisions and to start wars.
nato: NATO has its roots in the Atlantic Charter, a 1941 agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom. On 4 March 1947 France and the United Kingdom signed the Treaty of Dunkirk, an alliance against a possible attack by Germany, and in March 1948 the Treaty of Brussels extended it to the Benelux countries as the Brussels Treaty Organization, commonly called the Western Union.

Talks on a wider alliance including North America began that month, shaped by the Truman Doctrine of 1947 and the February 1948 coup d'état in Czechoslovakia, and led to the North Atlantic Treaty, signed at Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve founding members: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, the United Kingdom and the United States.

The treaty was largely dormant until the Korean War led to an integrated military structure. Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe was formed in 1951, the post of Secretary General was created in 1952, and Greece and Turkey joined that year. West Germany joined in May 1955, a major factor in the creation of the Soviet-dominated Warsaw Pact. Doubts about the credibility of NATO's defence led France to leave the military structure in 1966; it returned to the integrated command in 2009.

NATO conducted no military operations during the Cold War. In the Bosnian War it began enforcing a United Nations no-fly zone on 12 April 1993. After the Srebrenica genocide, a two-week bombing campaign, Operation Deliberate Force, began in August 1995 against the Army of the Republika Srpska, and the Dayton Agreement followed in November 1995. NATO then deployed a peacekeeping force, IFOR, of almost 60,000 troops.

The treaty's central provision is that an armed attack on one member is an attack on all. Under Article 6 the area within which an attack permits that response includes member territory in Europe and North America, Turkey, and the islands of the North Atlantic north of the Tropic of Cancer. The main headquarters are in Brussels. Twelve of the present 32 members joined in 1949; the other twenty joined in ten rounds of enlargement.
naypyidaw: Naypyidaw lies between the Bago Yoma and Shan Yoma mountain ranges, near the town of Pyinmana, about 320 kilometres north of Yangon. The name is Burmese for abode of the king, generally translated as royal capital, seat of the king or abode of kings. It was traditionally used as a suffix to the names of royal capitals; Mandalay, for example, was called Yadanabon Naypyidaw. Pyinmana is a long-standing settlement and had been a pre-colonial governorship dating to the Pagan kingdom era.

The city was founded on a greenfield site, and construction began in 2002 and was completed by 2012. Military projects were overseen by the Quartermaster General Tin Aung Myint Oo and civilian ones by an army colonel, Thein Nyunt. Three main groups built the city: the military's engineering corps, contractors with family ties to high-ranking military officials, and the military conglomerate Myanma Economic Holdings Limited. One estimate puts the cost at between 3 and 4 billion US dollars, only part of it in cash.

Naypyidaw officially replaced Yangon as the administrative capital on 6 November 2005. On 27 March 2006, Armed Forces Day, more than 12,000 troops marched in the new capital in its first public event, a military parade held on a concrete parade ground with large sculptures of Kings Anawrahta, Bayinnaung and Alaungpaya. The official name was announced during these ceremonies.

Several reasons have been suggested for the move. Naypyidaw is more central than Yangon and a transport hub next to the Shan, Kayah and Kayin states, where a stronger government and military presence was thought to bring stability. The official explanation was that Yangon had become too congested to allow government offices to expand. The historian Michael Aung-Thwin suggests that the move was a return to the Dry Zone, where Burmese royal capitals had traditionally been placed over a millennium.

Naypyidaw is the capital and third-largest city of Myanmar. It is unusual among the country's cities in being an entirely planned city and not part of any state or region. It is the seat of the Assembly of the Union, the Supreme Court and the Presidential Palace, and has separate zones for ministries, residences, the military, diplomats and hotels. It combines a large area with very low population density, and its roads are largely empty. The Uppatasanti Pagoda, completed in 2009, is only 30 centimetres shorter than the Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon.
nazareth: Nazareth lies in Lower Galilee, in a natural bowl that rises from about 320 metres above sea level to the crest of the surrounding hills at about 488 metres. The town is about 25 kilometres from the Sea of Galilee and about 9 kilometres west of Mount Tabor. Finds in the neighbouring Qafzeh Cave show that the area was populated in prehistoric times, and archaeological evidence shows that Nazareth itself was occupied from the late Hellenistic period through the Roman and into the Byzantine period.

According to the Gospel of Luke, Nazareth was the home village of Mary and the site of the Annunciation, and in the Gospel of Matthew Joseph and Mary settled there after the flight to Egypt. Craig S. Keener notes that it is rarely disputed that Jesus came from Nazareth, an obscure small village not worthy of invention. The earliest non-scriptural reference dates from about 221, and the town was Jewish until the 7th century. Bishop Arculf saw two churches there around 670.

Tancred established the city as the capital of the Principality of Galilee during the Crusades, when it became important. It declined under Mamluk rule, and after the Ottoman conquest its Christian residents were expelled, returning once the Druze emir Fakhr ad-Dīn II permitted it. In 1620 he allowed the Franciscans to build a small church at the Grotto of the Annunciation. In the 18th century Daher al-Umar made Nazareth a large town by encouraging immigration, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries European powers invested in churches, monasteries and schools.

Nazareth is the largest city in the Northern District of Israel, with a population of 75,704 in 2024, mostly Arabs, of whom 69 per cent are Muslim and 31 per cent Christian. It has been a centre of Christian pilgrimage since late antiquity. The Church of the Annunciation contains the Grotto of the Annunciation, where Catholic tradition holds that the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary; Greek Orthodox belief places that event at the Church of St Gabriel. The White Mosque is the oldest mosque in Nazareth.
nazism: Historians trace the roots of Nazism to European political culture before 1914. Almost all its essential elements, Martin Broszat points out, were present in the radical protest movements of pre-1914 Germany: a virulent antisemitism, a blood-and-soil ideology, the notion of a master race and the idea of territorial settlement in the East. Its ultranationalism came from pan-Germanism and the Völkisch movement, and the Freikorps paramilitary groups formed after Germany's defeat in the First World War were the source of its cult of violence. The idea of an Aryan race rested on 19th-century racial theories, among them those of Arthur de Gobineau.

Nazism, formally National Socialism, is the ideology of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. The German Workers' Party, founded in 1919, was renamed the National Socialist German Workers' Party in 1920, partly to use both left-wing and right-wing terms. Most scholars classify the ideology as far-right. It opposed liberal democracy and rejected Marxist class conflict, and advocated dictatorship under the Führerprinzip, the leader principle, set out in Hitler's Mein Kampf.

Its core was a belief in a racial hierarchy with an Aryan master race at the top. The Nazis treated Jews as a mixed race responsible for the exploitation of the Aryans and classed Slavs as subhuman. They sought a homogeneous community of the people, the Volksgemeinschaft, and aimed to unite all Germans and to gain land in Eastern Europe under the doctrine of Lebensraum.

The Nazi Party became the largest party in the German parliament in 1932, without a majority. In January 1933 President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor, with the support of conservative nationalists who believed they could control him. Through the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act the Nazis built a one-party state. Jews, Romani, political opponents and others were marginalised, imprisoned or murdered, and in the Second World War millions, among them two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, were killed in the Holocaust.

After Germany's defeat Nazism came to be widely regarded as evil. Only a few fringe racist groups, usually called neo-Nazis, describe themselves as its followers, and the use of Nazi symbols is illegal in many European countries.
ndjamena: N'Djamena lies on the Chari River in the south-west of Chad, near Lake Chad, in a flat and semi-arid landscape with a short wet season from June to September and a long dry season. It is a port at the confluence of the Logone and Chari rivers and forms a transborder agglomeration with Kousséri in Cameroon, on the west bank of both rivers, to which it is linked by a road bridge. The name comes from the Arabic Niǧāmīnā, place of rest, the name of a nearby village.

The French commander Émile Gentil founded Fort-Lamy on 29 May 1900, naming it after Amédée-François Lamy, an army officer killed in the Battle of Kousséri about a month earlier. It was at first a colonial outpost, and until the 1920s it was under French military rule. During the Second World War the French relied on its airport to move troops and supplies, and on 21 January 1942 a lone German Heinkel He 111 bombed the airfield, destroying oil supplies and ten aircraft. The city held its first municipal elections on 18 November 1956, when the European district had four seats on a thirty-three-seat council.

Chad became independent in 1960. On 6 April 1973 President François Tombalbaye renamed the city N'Djamena, as part of his authenticité programme of Africanization. It was partly destroyed in the Chadian Civil War in 1979 and 1980, when almost all of its population fled across the Chari to Kousséri and did not return until 1981–82. Rivalry between Goukouni Oueddei and Hissène Habré led to fighting that divided the city into sectors held by different warlords, until Libyan tanks entered at Goukouni's request. Libyan troops left in 1981, and Habré took the city with little resistance in 1982. In 1990 he was dislodged in a similar way by his former general Idriss Déby.

The city had 9,976 inhabitants in 1937, 18,435 in 1947, 126,483 in 1968 and 529,555 in 1993, and its population passed a million by the early 2010s. Much of the growth came from refugees seeking safety.

N'Djamena is the capital and largest city of Chad and a special status province divided into 10 districts. It is the seat of the National Assembly, the Supreme Court and every national ministry. Meat, fish and cotton processing are its chief industries, and it is a regional market for livestock, salt, dates and grains. The Chad National Museum holds the partial skull of Sahelanthropus, called Toumaï, found in the north of the country.
nelson-mandela: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was born on 18 July 1918 in the village of Mvezo, then part of South Africa's Cape Province. His forename Rolihlahla is a Xhosa term colloquially meaning troublemaker, and he later became known by his clan name, Madiba. His great-grandfather Ngubengcuka ruled the Thembu Kingdom, but Mandela's branch descended from a wife of the Ixhiba clan and so could not inherit the throne, though it was recognised as hereditary royal councillors. He studied law at the University of Fort Hare and the University of the Witwatersrand, joined the African National Congress (ANC) in 1943 and helped found its Youth League in 1944.

After the National Party government established apartheid, Mandela became President of the ANC's Transvaal branch and rose to prominence in the 1952 Defiance Campaign and the 1955 Congress of the People. He was prosecuted without success in the 1956 Treason Trial. Though at first committed to non-violent protest, he co-founded the militant Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961 and led a sabotage campaign. Police captured him on 5 August 1962, and he was later sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial.

Mandela served 27 years in prison, on Robben Island and then at Pollsmoor and Victor Verster prisons. President F. W. de Klerk released him in 1990. In July 1991 Mandela was elected ANC President, and in the election of 27 April 1994 he led the ANC to victory and became President of South Africa, the first black head of state. His government promulgated a new constitution and created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to investigate past human rights abuses.

Mandela declined a second term and retired in June 1999, succeeded by Thabo Mbeki. He founded the Nelson Mandela Foundation, which worked on rural development, school building and combating HIV/AIDS. He died on 5 December 2013. He received more than 250 honours, including the Nobel Peace Prize, and in South Africa he is often called Madiba and described as the Father of the Nation. Critics on the right denounced him as a communist terrorist, while some on the radical left thought him too ready to reconcile with apartheid's supporters.
neolithic: The term Neolithic, from the Greek for new and stone, was coined by John Lubbock in 1865 as a refinement of the three-age system. The wide-ranging developments of the period, which appear to have arisen independently in several parts of the world, were later called the Neolithic Revolution, a term coined in the 1920s by the archaeologist Vere Gordon Childe. In West Asia farming appeared about 12,000 years ago, and there the period lasted until the Chalcolithic, marked by metallurgy, from about 4500 BCE.

In the Levant the Neolithic arose from the Natufian culture, whose people had come to depend on wild cereals and had begun to live in one place. Climatic changes associated with the Younger Dryas are thought to have pushed them toward farming. The founder crops of the Fertile Crescent were wheat, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax.

The identifying feature of Neolithic technology is the use of polished or ground stone tools, in contrast to the flaked tools of the Paleolithic. The polished stone axe above all allowed forest to be cleared on a large scale. Farmers made sickle blades and grinding stones, and also pottery, beads and statuettes. Mud-brick houses coated with plaster began to appear, so that some have called the period the Age of Clay.

Most Neolithic societies were relatively simple and egalitarian, though more hierarchical than the Upper Paleolithic cultures before them. In Eurasia states generally arose only with metallurgy. Outside Eurasia, states formed during the local Neolithic in three areas: the Preceramic Andes with the Caral-Supe civilisation, Formative Mesoamerica and ancient Hawaiʻi.

The Neolithic spread unevenly. Farming appeared in south-east Europe in the 7th millennium BCE, and archaeogenetics has shown that its spread to Europe was strongly tied to the migration of early farmers from Anatolia about 9,000 years ago. In north-west Europe the Neolithic began much later, from about 4500 BCE to 1700 BCE. In Egypt it lasted until about 3150 BCE, and in China until about 2000 BCE.

In Africa south of the Sahara the first food production was mobile herding, and archaeologists speak of a Pastoral Neolithic. In the Americas different terms are used, such as the Formative stage. Australia is generally held not to have had a Neolithic period. The temple of Ġgantija on Gozo is described as the oldest known freestanding structure.
nepal: Nepal is a landlocked, roughly trapezoidal country about 800 kilometres long and 200 kilometres wide, with an area of 147,516 square kilometres. It lies mainly in the Himalayas but includes a small strip of the Indo-Gangetic Plain in the south. Eight of the world's ten highest mountains stand there, among them Mount Everest. The Himalayas rose from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, which began about 75 million years ago, and lakes held back by the rising ranges broke through as late as 100,000 years ago, leaving fertile valleys such as the Kathmandu Valley. Kathmandu is the capital and largest city.

The oldest archaeological evidence of human settlement in Nepal dates to about 30,000 years ago. Around 600 BCE small kingdoms and confederations of clans arose in the south, and from one of them, the Shakya polity, came the prince who became Gautama Buddha, traditionally dated 563 to 483 BCE. By 250 BCE the southern regions were under Maurya influence. The emperor Ashoka made a pilgrimage to Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace according to Buddhist tradition, and the inscription on the pillar he raised marks the starting point of properly recorded Nepalese history. By the 4th century CE much of Nepal was under the Gupta Empire.

The Kathmandu Valley was the seat of the Newar confederacy known as Nepal Mandala, and its traders dominated the Himalayan branch of the Silk Road. By the 18th century the Gorkha Kingdom had unified Nepal under the Shah dynasty. The country was never colonised, but after the treaty of Sugauli it served as a buffer state between Imperial China and British India, and the Rana dynasty of premiers allied with the British Empire.

Parliamentary democracy was introduced in 1951 after the Nepali Congress overthrew the Rana regime. King Mahendra started the partyless Panchayat system in 1962, and monarchs suspended parliamentary democracy in 1960 and 2005. The Nepalese Civil War ended with a secular republic in 2008, ending the world's last Hindu monarchy, and the Constitution of 2015 made Nepal a federal parliamentary republic of seven provinces.

The 2021 census counted 29.5 million people in 125 ethnic groups speaking 123 mother tongues. The Nepali are descended from four major migrations, and among the earliest inhabitants were the Kirat of the east, the Newars of the Kathmandu Valley and the Tharus of the Terai. Nepal declared untouchability illegal in 1963.
nero: Nero was born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus on 15 December 37 at Antium, the only child of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Agrippina the Younger. His uncle was the reigning emperor Caligula, and through his mother he was a descendant of Augustus. His father died when he was three. By the time he was eleven, his mother had married the emperor Claudius, who adopted him as his heir. When Claudius died in 54, Nero came to the throne at the age of sixteen with the backing of the Praetorian Guard and the Senate.

In his early years Nero was guided by his mother, his tutor Seneca the Younger and the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus. His first speech to the Senate, prepared by Seneca, promised to end secret trials and to respect the privileges of senators. Agrippina meant to rule through her son, and the struggle between them ended with her murder in 59. Roman sources also implicate him in the deaths of his stepbrother Britannicus and his wife Claudia Octavia. Modern scholars think the reign went well before Agrippina's death, and a successful expedition explored the sources of the Nile.

The general Corbulo fought the Roman–Parthian War of 58 to 63 and made peace with Parthia. Suetonius Paulinus defeated a major revolt in Britain led by Queen Boudica, who had burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium. The Great Fire of Rome began on the night of 18 to 19 July 64 and destroyed three of the city's fourteen districts and severely damaged seven more. Suetonius records a belief that Nero started it to clear land for his Golden House, and Tacitus says he seized Christians as scapegoats and had them burned alive. In 65 a conspiracy led by Gaius Calpurnius Piso failed, and Seneca and the poet Lucan were among those who died. The First Jewish–Roman War began in 66.

In March 68 Gaius Julius Vindex, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, rebelled against Nero's tax policies and called on Servius Sulpicius Galba to declare himself emperor. Verginius Rufus defeated Vindex at Vesontio in May, but support for Galba grew, the Praetorian prefect Nymphidius Sabinus deserted Nero, and he was declared a public enemy. Nero fled Rome and killed himself in 68, which began the civil wars of the Year of the Four Emperors.

Most surviving sources, chiefly Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio, are hostile, but none was written during his reign, and some modern historians question their reliability, noting his popularity among ordinary Romans. In the eastern provinces a legend arose that he had not died, and at least three leaders of short-lived rebellions presented themselves as Nero reborn.
nevada: Nevada is a landlocked state in the Western United States. It borders Idaho to the northeast, Oregon to the northwest, California to the west, Arizona to the southeast and Utah to the east. Almost the whole state lies within the Basin and Range Province, broken up by many north-south mountain ranges with endorheic valleys between them. Nevada comprises most of the Great Basin as well as a large part of the Mojave Desert.

The Sierra Nevada lies in the rain shadow to the west, and Nevada is the driest state in the country. The Humboldt River crosses the north from east to west and ends in the Humboldt Sink near Lovelock. The Walker, Truckee and Carson rivers run eastward from the Sierra Nevada and end in Walker Lake, Pyramid Lake and the Carson Sink. The Colorado River forms much of the boundary with Arizona and drains much of the south.

The earliest inhabitants included the Goshute, Southern Paiute, Mohave and Washoe peoples. Francisco Garcés was the first European in the area, which was claimed as part of the Spanish Empire and belonged to the Viceroyalty of New Spain. It became part of the province of Alta California in 1804, when the Californias were split. After the Mexican War of Independence was won in 1821, Alta California became a territory of Mexico with a small population.

The United States annexed the area in 1848 after its victory in the Mexican-American War, and in 1850 it was incorporated into the New Mexico and Utah territories. The discovery of silver at the Comstock Lode in 1859 caused a population boom and became an impetus for the creation of Nevada Territory out of western Utah Territory in 1861. Nevada became the 36th state on 31 October 1864, the second of two states added to the Union during the Civil War after West Virginia. For that reason it is called the Battle Born State.

In 1940, with just over 110,000 people, Nevada was by far the least populated state. Legalized gambling and lenient marriage and divorce laws then made it a major tourist destination. Las Vegas grew from a gulch of 100 people in 1900 to 10,000 by 1950 and 100,000 by 1970.

The capital is Carson City and the largest city is Las Vegas. The state's name is Spanish for snowy, and its official nickname is the Silver State because of silver's historical importance to its economy. The 2020 census counted 3,104,614 people, nearly three-quarters of them in Clark County, which contains the Las Vegas-Paradise metropolitan area. Tourism is the largest employer, and mining remains a substantial sector, with gold the most valuable mineral. About 80 per cent of the land is managed by the United States federal government.
new-delhi: New Delhi lies on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, on the floodplain of the Yamuna River, and there is little difference in elevation across the city. The area was once part of the Aravali Range, of which the Delhi Ridge, sometimes called the Lungs of Delhi, is all that remains. The municipality covers 42.7 square kilometres and forms a small part of the larger metropolitan area of Delhi. In everyday speech Delhi and New Delhi are often used interchangeably, although they are distinct administrative entities.

Under British rule Calcutta was the capital of India until December 1911. It had become a centre of nationalist movements from the late nineteenth century, and Viceroy Curzon's partition of Bengal produced a large upsurge in political activity, including assassinations of British officials, and a boycott of British goods. The colonial government reunited Bengal and moved the capital. Old Delhi had been the political centre of several empires, among them the Delhi Sultanate and, from 1649 to 1857, the Mughal Empire. The British government of India also judged that Delhi, in the centre of northern India, would be logistically easier to govern from.

George V laid the foundation stone of New Delhi, south of the old city, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. The land was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act of 1894. The city was designed by the British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker and took about twenty years to build. Viceroy Irwin inaugurated it on 13 February 1931.

The plan was chosen above all to be a symbol of British power and supremacy. Its architecture follows a British Classical and Palladian tradition, with some Hindu and Islamic features that were included through the persistence of Viceroy Hardinge and historians such as E. B. Havell. The city is structured around two promenades, the Rajpath, or King's Way, which runs from the Rashtrapati Bhavan, formerly the Viceroy's House, on Raisina Hill to India Gate, and the Janpath, which crosses it at right angles.

New Delhi is the capital of India and the seat of all three branches of its government, with the Rashtrapati Bhavan, Parliament House and the Supreme Court. It is part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi and is administered by the New Delhi Municipal Council. Hindi is the most widely spoken language and English is the main formal language of business and government. The city has about 145 foreign embassies and high commissions, and many regional offices of United Nations bodies. The National Museum, formally inaugurated on 15 August 1949, holds about 200,000 works of art covering over 5,000 years.
new-guinea: New Guinea, also known as Papua, has an area of 785,753 km2. It lies in Melanesia, in the southwestern Pacific, separated from Australia by the 150-kilometre-wide Torres Strait. Both landmasses lie on the same continental shelf and were joined in the Pleistocene, when sea levels were low, as the landmass of Sahul. The island has the third-largest remaining rainforest in the world and the highest plant biodiversity of any island. Its shape is often compared to that of a bird-of-paradise, giving the names Bird's Head Peninsula in the northwest and Bird's Tail Peninsula in the southeast. The Spanish explorer Íñigo Ortiz de Retes gave the island its name in 1545, because its peoples seemed to him to resemble those of Guinea in Africa.

Humans arrived on New Guinea perhaps 60,000 years ago, probably by sea from Southeast Asia during the last glacial period, although the date is debated. Their descendants developed one of the earliest known agricultures: the highlands were an early and independent centre of agriculture, with evidence of irrigation going back at least 10,000 years, and sugarcane was cultivated around 6000 BCE. Today almost a thousand tribal groups live on the island, with a near-equivalent number of languages, making it the most linguistically diverse area in the world.

The western part of the island had contact with kingdoms elsewhere in the Indonesian region; the Negarakertagama mentions Wanin and Sran as part of Majapahit's tributary. The sultans of Tidore claimed sovereignty over various coastal areas, whose exports included resins, spices, slaves and the highly prized feathers of the bird-of-paradise. In the 1780s Sultan Nuku of Tidore, who rebelled against Dutch colonisation, called himself Sultan of Tidore and Papua. After Tidore became a Dutch tributary, much of its claimed territory came under Dutch rule as part of the Dutch East Indies.

Portuguese and Spanish sailors made the first known European contact in the 16th century. Jorge de Menezes saw the western tip in 1526-27 and named it ilhas dos Papuas, and in 1606 Luís Vaz de Torres explored the southern coast. In 1942 the Japanese invaded the Dutch territory and the Australian territories in the eastern half. The highlands, northern and eastern parts became key battlefields, including those for Port Moresby, Milne Bay and the Kokoda track. Papuans often gave vital help to the Allies, and about 216,000 Japanese, Australian and U.S. servicemen died in the New Guinea campaign.

The island is divided politically into roughly equal halves along a north-south line. The eastern half is the mainland of Papua New Guinea, independent since 1975 and formerly administered by Australia. The western half, formerly Dutch, is divided into six Indonesian provinces. The two major cities on the island are Port Moresby and Jayapura.
new-hampshire: New Hampshire is part of the six-state New England region. It is bounded by Quebec to the north and north-west, Maine and the Gulf of Maine to the east, Massachusetts to the south and Vermont to the west. Its main regions include the Great North Woods, the White Mountains, the Lakes Region, the Seacoast and the Merrimack Valley. It has the shortest ocean coastline of any coastal state in the United States, 18 miles (29 km).

The White Mountains span the north-central part of the state and include Mount Washington, at 6,288 feet (1,917 m) the tallest peak in the north-eastern United States. The Old Man of the Mountain, a face-like rock profile in Franconia Notch, disintegrated in May 2003 but remains a symbol of the state.

Algonquian-speaking Abenaki peoples, largely divided between the Androscoggin, Cowasuck and Pennacook nations, inhabited the area before European colonisation. English and French explorers visited in 1600–1605, and David Thompson settled at Odiorne's Point in present-day Rye in 1623. The first permanent European settlement was at Hilton's Point, present-day Dover. After several years of petitions from Robert Tufton Mason, the colony became a Royal Province in 1679, the first in New England. Dover and Durham were burned in 1689 and 1692 during King William's War.

New Hampshire was one of the Thirteen Colonies that rebelled against British rule. In 1774 its people seized Fort William and Mary from the British, and in 1776 it became the first of the colonies to establish an independent government and state constitution. In 1788 it was the ninth state to ratify the United States Constitution, bringing it into effect. It was an active centre of abolitionism and fielded close to 32,000 Union soldiers in the Civil War. Rapid industrialisation followed, and the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company in Manchester was the largest cotton textile plant in the world.

Concord is the state capital and Manchester the most populous city, and the state has 1,377,529 residents. Its motto, Live Free or Die, reflects its role in the Revolutionary War, and its nickname, the Granite State, refers to its granite formations and quarries. French Canadians formed the most significant influx of immigrants, and a quarter of residents have French American ancestry. The state constitution of 1783 is its supreme law.
new-jersey: New Jersey lies between the Hudson and Delaware rivers. It is bordered to the north and northeast by New York, to the east and southeast by the Atlantic Ocean, to the west by the Delaware River and Pennsylvania, and to the southwest by Delaware Bay and Delaware. At 7,354 square miles (19,050 km2) it is the fifth-smallest state by land area. It is broadly divided into North, Central and South Jersey, with the Jersey Shore along the Atlantic coast.

Pressure from the collision of North America and Africa gave rise to the Appalachian Mountains. Around 18,000 years ago glaciers reached New Jersey, and as they retreated they left behind Lake Passaic along with rivers, meadows, swamps and gorges.

People have lived in New Jersey since the 6th millennium BCE, beginning with the Lenape, whose name for the land is Scheyichbi. The Lenape were several autonomous groups who practised maize agriculture to supplement hunting and gathering around the Delaware River, the lower Hudson River and western Long Island Sound. They were divided into matrilineal clans grouped in three phratries identified by the animal signs Turtle, Turkey and Wolf. They first met the Dutch in the early 17th century, and their main dealings with the Dutch and later settlers were through the fur trade.

Dutch and Swedish colonists founded the first European settlements. The British later seized control and established the Province of New Jersey, named after the Channel Island of Jersey. The colony's fertile lands and relative religious tolerance drew a large and diverse population. New Jersey was among the Thirteen Colonies that supported the American Revolution and hosted several pivotal battles and military commands in the American Revolutionary War, which earned it the title Crossroads of the American Revolution. It remained in the Union during the American Civil War.

The state capital is Trenton and the most populous city is Newark. The 2020 census counted 9,288,994 residents, and New Jersey has the highest population density of any state. It lies at the centre of the Northeast megalopolis, and its central position helped fuel rapid growth and suburbanization in the second half of the 20th century. It is home to Princeton University and to Rutgers University, headquartered in New Brunswick. Among inventions credited to the state are FM radio, the motion picture camera, the light bulb, the phonograph and the transistor.
new-mexico: New Mexico is a landlocked state in the south-west, sharing the Four Corners region with Utah, Colorado and Arizona. The Rio Grande and its valley run north to south through the centre. The Sangre de Cristo Mountains lie east of the river in the north, the Great Plains reach into the eastern third, the Colorado Plateau dominates the north-west, and the Chihuahuan Desert extends through the south. The landscape is more varied than its popular image as arid desert.

The name was given long before present-day Mexico took it in 1821. After the Spanish conquered the Aztecs in the early 16th century, they called the region they began to explore Nuevo México, after the Kingdom of Mexico. In 1581 the Chamuscado and Rodríguez Expedition named the area north of the Rio Grande San Felipe del Nuevo México. The Spaniards had hoped to find wealthy cultures like the Mexica, but the cultures proved unrelated and lacking in riches.

The first known inhabitants were the Clovis culture of Paleo-Indians. Later came the Mogollon and the Ancestral Pueblo cultures, known for sophisticated pottery and urban development, with pueblos or remains at Acoma, Taos and Chaco Culture National Historical Park. The Navajo and Apache arrived in the late 1400s.

Esteban de Dorantes was the first person from the Old World to reach New Mexico, in 1539, and was killed by Pueblo peoples. Juan de Oñate y Salazar began Spanish colonisation in 1598. In the Ácoma Massacre of 1599 his army set fire to Acoma Pueblo and approximately 800 to 1,000 Ácoma were killed, and Oñate then ordered that the right foot of every man over 25 be cut off. Santa Fe was founded in 1610 as the government seat of Nuevo México in New Spain.

The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 was the first successful revolution against colonial rule in the Americas. Spanish rule returned in 1692. After Mexican independence in 1821 the province became an autonomous territory, and the United States annexed it after the Mexican–American War in 1848. New Mexico was a territory for 64 years and became the 47th state on 6 January 1912. It hosted key facilities of the Manhattan Project and was the site of the first nuclear test, Trinity, in 1945.

Santa Fe is the capital, the oldest state capital in the United States, and Albuquerque is the largest city. The state is home to one-third of the Navajo Nation, 19 federally recognised Pueblo communities and three federally recognised Apache tribes.
new-orleans: New Orleans lies in the Mississippi River Delta, south of Lake Pontchartrain, on the banks of the Mississippi about 105 miles upriver from the Gulf of Mexico. It was originally settled on the river's natural levees, the high ground, and after the Flood Control Act of 1965 the Army Corps of Engineers built levees around a much larger area that included former marshland. Half of the city is now at or below local mean sea level. Before European colonists arrived, the Choctaw called the area Bulbancha, meaning land of many tongues.

French colonists founded the city in 1718, and it was the territorial capital of French Louisiana. The Third Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800 restored French control of New Orleans and Louisiana, and Napoleon sold both to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The city then grew rapidly with Americans, French, Creoles and Africans, and later with Irish, Germans, Poles and Italians. Sugar and cotton were cultivated with slave labour on large plantations nearby.

In the last campaign of the War of 1812 a British force of 11,000 tried to capture the city, and Andrew Jackson, leading militia, regulars and local privateers under Jean Lafitte, defeated it in the Battle of New Orleans on 8 January 1815. The Treaty of Ghent had been signed already, but neither army had learned of it.

In April 1862 the Union Navy occupied the city, and General Benjamin F. Butler became military governor. After the war a legislative amendment of 1889 with a grandfather clause effectively disfranchised freedmen, and public schools remained segregated until 1960. The city was the fifth-largest in the country in 1860, but after the mid-19th century growth shifted elsewhere as railways and highways reduced river traffic.

On 29 August 2005 the federal levee system failed during Hurricane Katrina, and about 80 percent of the city flooded. More than 1,300 people died, thousands of residents were displaced, and the population fell by over 50 percent.

New Orleans is a consolidated city and parish, coextensive with Orleans Parish, and the most populous city in Louisiana, with 383,997 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It remains a major port and commercial hub for the Gulf Coast, with a maritime industry and petrochemical production nearby. The French Quarter, its historic heart, is known for French and Spanish Creole architecture. The city is known for its music, Creole cuisine and the Mardi Gras celebrations, and its strong Roman Catholic tradition goes back to its French and Spanish settlement.
new-testament: The New Testament was written in Koine Greek by various authors, although the historical Jesus is generally agreed to have spoken primarily Aramaic. Its books are thought to have been written by Jewish Christians living in the Roman Empire under Roman occupation. The author of the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles is frequently regarded as an exception, and scholars are divided on whether he was a Gentile or a Hellenistic Jew.

Literary analysis suggests that many of its texts were written in the mid-to-late first century, and there is no scholarly consensus on the date of the latest text. Some scholars date many or all of the books before 70 CE, while others date some texts much later. Richard Pervo dated Luke–Acts to about 115 CE, and David Trobisch places Acts in the mid-to-late second century.

The collection has 27 texts: four gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, epistles attributed to Paul and other authors, and the Book of Revelation. Each gospel narrates the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth. The word gospel derives from the Old English gōd-spell, meaning good news, and the Greek equivalent is euangélion. Beginning in the late second century the four accounts were called the Gospel according to a named author. The first author to name the canonical gospels explicitly was Irenaeus of Lyon, in his book Against Heresies, written around 180.

The order of the books differs between traditions. In the Latin West, before the Vulgate, the Gospels stood in the order Matthew, John, Luke and Mark. An early edition of Paul's letters was arranged from longest to shortest, and Hebrews was placed in different positions within it. The 16th-century Luther Bible places Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation last, which reflects Martin Luther's views on their canonicity.

The canon developed gradually. In the first centuries many books were widely considered inspired, but no single canon was formally recognised. About 140 CE Marcion accepted only a version of Luke and ten of Paul's letters, and rejected the Old Testament entirely. Most other Christians rejected his canon, and scholars such as Adolf von Harnack and David Trobisch have argued that the church formed its own canon partly in response to him. The 27-book canon was formalised by the late fourth century.

The text was transmitted in manuscripts, now numbering in the thousands, which contain variants. The earliest date from the late second to early third centuries, with Papyrus 52 a possible exception. Textual criticism uses them to reconstruct the earliest recoverable text. Catholics, Orthodox, evangelicals and many other Protestants regard it as inspired scripture. Catholics and Orthodox receive it together with sacred tradition, whereas Protestants hold that doctrine is to be derived from scripture alone.
new-zealand: New Zealand comprises two main islands, the North Island (Te Ika-a-Māui) and the South Island (Te Waipounamu), and more than 700 smaller islands. They are separated by Cook Strait, 22 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. The country is long and narrow, with about 15,000 kilometres of coastline and a land area of 268,000 square kilometres, and its exclusive economic zone covers more than 15 times its land area.

The Southern Alps divide the South Island along its length; Aoraki / Mount Cook, at 3,724 metres, is the highest of 18 peaks over 3,000 metres. The North Island is marked by volcanism, and the Taupō Volcanic Zone has formed a large plateau, with Mount Ruapehu its highest mountain and Lake Taupō, the largest lake, in the caldera of one of the world's most active supervolcanoes. New Zealand is prone to earthquakes.

The first people to reach the islands were Polynesians in oceangoing waka, believed to have arrived in several waves between about 1280 and 1350. According to most Māori oral traditions, the explorer Kupe first discovered the islands, followed by a great fleet from Hawaiki. The belief in a single great fleet has since been superseded by the view that settlement was a planned event spread over several decades. No remains, artefacts or structures can be reliably dated earlier than the Kaharoa eruption of Mount Tarawera around 1314.

Abel Tasman's crew met a hostile reception from Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri in 1642, and four of his crew were killed. Europeans did not return until James Cook mapped almost the entire coastline in 1769. The potato and the musket transformed Māori agriculture and warfare, and the intertribal Musket Wars covered over 600 battles between 1801 and 1840, killing 30,000 to 40,000 Māori. The Māori population fell to around 40% of its pre-contact level during the 19th century, with introduced diseases the major factor.

New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary democracy, though its constitution is not codified. The upper house, the Legislative Council, was abolished in 1950. The 2023 census enumerated a resident population of 4,993,923, and 84.5% of the population lives in urban areas. Around 80% of New Zealanders are of European descent and 15% Māori.

From the early 20th century until the late 1960s Māori culture was suppressed by the attempted assimilation of Māori into British New Zealanders. Since the mid-1980s the economy has moved from a protectionist and highly regulated model to a liberalised free-trade economy. Aotearoa, often translated as land of the long white cloud, is the present Māori name for the country.
niamey: Niamey lies in the western part of Niger, surrounded by the Tillabéri Region, mostly on the plateau of the left bank of the Niger River, with a few developments on the alluvial plain of the right bank. At the core of the Sahel it has a hot semi-arid climate, with monthly highs from 32 °C in January to 41 °C in April, and an annual rainfall of 500 to 750 millimetres falling mostly between early June and early September. The Niger is the city's only permanent river.

The area was of little importance before the colonial era and served as a buffer zone between the Sahelian kingdoms. In the late sixteenth century its residents included Zarma and other Songhai refugees from the Moroccan invasion of the Songhai Empire, Hausa-speaking Maouri hunters and the Fula. French forces began their invasion of Niger in 1891. The first European mentions of Niamey come from the 1897 mission of Émile Auguste Léon Hourst and the 1899 Voulet–Chanoine Mission, which set fire to it. Captain Henri Salaman established a military post there in 1901.

Niamey replaced Zinder as the territorial capital from 1903 to 1911 and again in 1926, after which large-scale development followed. The first city plan, in 1930, relocated neighbourhoods and segregated European and indigenous districts, which remained separate until the 1950s. In 1956 Niamey held Niger's first municipal elections and elected Djibo Bakary as its first mayor. Its population had reached 33,816 by 1960, the year of independence. In the 1970s and 1980s growth was fuelled by the national uranium boom and by droughts that brought rural migrants.

Niamey is the capital and largest city of Niger and its main economic centre, with a large informal economy and extensive urban agriculture. The languages of its two largest peoples, Zarma and Hausa, serve as lingua francas. The city is divided into five communes, four on the left bank and one on the right, and is home to Abdou Moumouni University and the Niamey National Hospital. The 2022 estimate gave it 1,407,635 inhabitants.
niccolo-machiavelli: Niccolò di Bernardo dei Machiavelli was born in Florence on 3 May 1469, the third child and first son of the attorney Bernardo di Niccolò Machiavelli and Bartolomea di Stefano Nelli. His father was born illegitimate and so could not become a full citizen of Florence or take part in its politics, which also affected Niccolò, who could not obtain full citizenship rights.

He grew up in a tumultuous era. At eight he saw the violence that followed the Pazzi conspiracy, which aimed to kill Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici in a church; only Giuliano died. As a young man he heard the sermons of Girolamo Savonarola but was not swayed. In 1494 Florence restored the republic and expelled the Medici, who had ruled for some sixty years.

Machiavelli's civil service began shortly after Savonarola was burned at the stake for heresy. For many years he served as a senior official in the Florentine Republic with responsibilities in diplomatic and military affairs, working as secretary to the second chancery from 1498 to 1512, while the Medici were out of power.

When the Medici retook power in 1512 he was expelled from his duties. Soon afterwards he was mistakenly suspected of treason and sent into exile. A year later he took up the life of a political writer. He died on 21 June 1527.

His best-known book, The Prince (Il Principe), was written around 1513 but not published until 1532, five years after his death. It addresses not only hereditary princes but also new princes who have founded their own dynasties, and holds that the virtues commonly recommended to rulers can hinder them. A ruler must be willing to act unscrupulously when necessary. He held that it was better for a ruler to be widely feared than greatly loved, and that violence may be needed to stabilise power. The saying that the ends justify the means is often wrongly attributed to him.

The Discourses on Livy, composed c. 1517, is said to have paved the way for modern republicanism, and his works influenced Enlightenment authors such as Jean-Jacques Rousseau and James Harrington. His name came to evoke unscrupulous acts, and commentators such as Leo Strauss have called him a teacher of evil. Scholars disagree on whether his works form a coherent system and whether he was a philosopher proper, and he is often called the father of modern political philosophy and political science.
nice: Nice lies on the French Riviera, at the foot of the French Alps, about 13 kilometres west of Monaco and 30 kilometres west of the French–Italian border. It consists of two large bays, and the city rises from the flat beach into gentle hills bounded by mountains that mark the southern and nearly the western edge of the Ligurian Alps. The Terra Amata archaeological site shows early use of fire and the construction of houses. The settlement of Nikaia was probably founded around 350 BCE and named for Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, in honour of a victory over the neighbouring Ligurians.

Nikaia became one of the busiest trading ports on the Ligurian coast, with a rival in the Roman town of Cemenelum, whose ruins are in the district of Cimiez. It repulsed the Saracens in 729, but they pillaged and burned it in 859 and again in 880 and held the surrounding country for most of the 10th century. In the Middle Ages the city, as an ally of Pisa, was the enemy of Genoa, and it kept its municipal liberties despite attempts by the King of France and the Holy Roman Emperor to subjugate it.

In 1388 the commune placed itself under the protection of the Counts of Savoy, becoming the County of Nice. In 1561 Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, replaced Latin with Italian as the language of government. The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 gave the city back to the Duke of Savoy. The armies of the French First Republic conquered the county in 1792, and it reverted to the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia in 1814.

The Treaty of Turin of 1860, signed by the Sardinian king and Napoleon III, ceded the county to France as a reward for French help in the Second Italian War of Independence. A plebiscite was held on 15 and 16 April 1860, and the yes vote won 86 percent in Nice. Opponents of annexation called for abstention, and the result is described as partly due to pressure from the authorities.

Nice is the prefecture of the Alpes-Maritimes department in the region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur. From the second half of the 18th century English aristocratic families began to spend their winters there, and the Promenade des Anglais, inaugurated in its refurbished form in 1931, takes its name from these visitors, who included Queen Victoria. Marc Chagall and Henri Matisse are commemorated in the city's museums. UNESCO proclaimed Nice a World Heritage Site in 2021 for its history as a winter resort.
nicholas-ii: Nicholas II was born on 18 May 1868 (6 May in the Old Style calendar) at the Alexander Palace in Tsarskoye Selo, the eldest child of the future Emperor Alexander III and Maria Feodorovna, born Princess Dagmar of Denmark. He was educated privately and trained for military service, though he was widely considered ill-prepared to rule. He became heir apparent on 1 March 1881, when his grandfather Alexander II was assassinated by the Narodnaya Volya. In April 1894 he proposed to Alix of Hesse at Coburg, and they were engaged on 20 April. He became emperor on 1 November 1894, when his father died.

Nicholas believed that his authority came from God and that his duty was to keep his absolute power intact. Early in his reign a deputation of zemstvo representatives presented the Tver Address, proposing constitutional reform, and he rejected it. He pursued an aggressive policy in Manchuria and Korea, which led to the Russo-Japanese War. Defeat, together with the demonstrations shot on Bloody Sunday in January 1905, fed the Revolution of 1905. On 5 August 1905 he issued a manifesto convening the State Duma, and in the October Manifesto he pledged civil liberties and a Duma with legislative powers. The 1906 constitution nevertheless described him as the supreme autocrat, and ministers answered only to him.

In 1904 his son Alexei was born, who had haemophilia, an illness that complicated the question of the succession. In 1907 the Anglo-Russian Convention settled central Asian disputes with Britain and led to the Triple Entente. The government condemned the Kishinev pogrom, though in private Nicholas reportedly admired the mobs. His Russification measures in Finland, begun with the February Manifesto of 1899, were deeply unpopular.

In the First World War Nicholas took command at the front in 1915, leaving the capital to intrigue and strikes, and the failure to supply the army and the population brought riots and mutinies. He abdicated in March 1917, ending 304 years of Romanov rule, and tried to pass the throne to his brother Michael.

Britain offered the family asylum on 19 March 1917 but withdrew the offer in April. The family was held first at Tsarskoye Selo, then in Bolshevik custody, and was executed at Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918. Their remains were reburied in Saint Petersburg in 1998, and in 2000 the Russian Orthodox Church canonised them as passion bearers. The majority view among historians is that he was well-intentioned but a poor ruler.
nicolaus-copernicus: Nicolaus Copernicus was born on 19 February 1473 in Thorn (Toruń), in Royal Prussia, a semi-autonomous and multilingual region of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland. His parents were German-speaking. His father was a merchant from Kraków, and his mother was the daughter of a wealthy Thorn merchant. He was the youngest of four children. His brother Andreas became an Augustinian canon at Frauenburg (Frombork), and his sister Barbara became a Benedictine nun.

His mother tongue was German, and he wrote most of his surviving works in Latin, the principal language of European scholarship. Whether he spoke Polish is uncertain, since the evidence is indirect. While studying canon law at the University of Bologna in 1496 he signed into the German student organisation, the Natio Germanorum.

Copernicus obtained a doctorate in canon law and was also a mathematician, astronomer, physician, classics scholar, translator, governor, diplomat and economist. From 1497 he was a canon of the Warmian Cathedral chapter. In 1517 he derived a quantity theory of money, a key concept in economics, and in 1519 he formulated an economic principle that later came to be called Gresham's law. He never married. He died on 24 May 1543, just after the publication of his book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres).

Copernicus formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its centre. Its publication in 1543 was a major event in the history of science, triggering the Copernican Revolution and contributing to the Scientific Revolution. A similar heliocentric model had been developed eighteen centuries earlier by Aristarchus of Samos, and Copernicus likely arrived at his model independently. In an early unpublished manuscript he mentioned the moving Earth theory of Philolaus, but he removed the reference from the published text.

The immediate result of publication was only mild controversy. The Council of Trent, which met from 1545 to 1563, did not discuss his theory. The Dominican Giovanni Maria Tolosani denounced Copernicanism in 1545, arguing that it was scientifically unproven because Copernicus assumed the motion of the Earth without offering a physical theory for it. The Catholic Church took no official action until about six decades after the book appeared.
nicosia: Nicosia stands on the fertile Mesaoria plain, in the rain shadow of the Troodos Mountains. Its climate is hot and semi-arid, with long, hot, dry summers and mild winters, and most of the rain falls in winter. The names Lefkosia in Greek and Lefkoşa in Turkish come from Leucosia, a form that became common in the Byzantine period and is usually interpreted as meaning the white estate. Earlier Greek sources in late antiquity gave several names built on the Greek words for white or poplar and for god, among them Leuteon, Leucon and Leucopolis.

Nicosia has been continuously inhabited since approximately 2500 BCE, near the onset of the Bronze Age, when the first settlers established themselves on the Mesaoria plain. The city-state of Ledra is associated with the area. Most Mycenaean-era ruins lie on the hill of Ayia Paraskevi, 6 km south-east of the centre, and Ledra is said to have been one of the twelve kingdoms of ancient Cyprus founded by the Achaeans after the Trojan War. The earliest written reference to the settlement is an Assyrian inscription of the reign of Esarhaddon (r. 681–669 BCE), on a clay prism of about 672 BCE, which records it as Lidir. Its ruler Onasagoras is recorded as having paid tribute to Esarhaddon.

By 330 BCE Ledra was a small town of little significance, economically and politically dependent on the nearby town of Chytri, with farming as the main occupation. It did not share the growth, driven by trade, of the Cypriot coastal towns. Some sources say Leucos, a son of Ptolemy I Soter of Egypt, restored it around 280 BCE, though one scholar dismissed this as an early modern fancy based only on speculation about the name. Nicosia has been the capital of Cyprus since the 10th century. In 1308 the Lusignan king Henry II of Jerusalem repaired the Benedictine Abbey of Our Lady of Tyre, one of the oldest Armenian churches, after an earthquake destroyed it.

Nicosia is the capital of Cyprus and its financial and main business centre, and the southeasternmost capital of any member state of the European Union. It is the last divided capital in Europe. After Cyprus became independent from British rule in 1960, the Bloody Christmas conflict of 1963 between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots set off intercommunal violence, and in 1964 the two communities separated into the south and north of the city. In 1974 Turkey invaded Cyprus days after a coup backed by the Greek junta, and the island was divided, with the dividing line running through Nicosia. The northern part is the de facto capital of Northern Cyprus. The city has the Cyprus Museum, the island's largest and oldest archaeological museum.
niels-bohr: Niels Henrik David Bohr was born in Copenhagen on 7 October 1885, the second of three children of Christian Bohr, Professor of Physiology at the University of Copenhagen, and Ellen Adler, daughter of the Danish Jewish banker David Baruch Adler.
