His younger brother Harald became a mathematician and played football for Denmark at the 1908 Summer Olympics. Niels enrolled at the University of Copenhagen in 1903 and studied physics under Christian Christiansen. In September 1911, with a Carlsberg Foundation fellowship, he went to Cambridge, where he failed to impress J. J. Thomson, and then to Manchester at the invitation of Ernest Rutherford.

Bohr proposed that the energy levels of electrons are discrete and that electrons revolve in stable orbits around the nucleus but can jump from one level to another. Later models have replaced it, though its underlying principles remain valid. He also conceived the principle of complementarity, that items can be analysed in terms of contradictory properties, such as behaving as a wave or as a stream of particles. This notion dominated his thinking in both science and philosophy.

In April 1917 he began a campaign for an Institute of Theoretical Physics, backed by the Danish government, the Carlsberg Foundation, industry and private donors. Legislation establishing it passed in November 1918, and he became its director. Now the Niels Bohr Institute, it was a focal point for quantum mechanics in the 1920s and 1930s, when most of the best-known theoretical physicists spent time there.

In 1933 Bohr offered refugees from Nazism temporary posts and financial support, and helped them find places, among them James Franck, Lise Meitner and Edward Teller. In September 1943 word reached him that the Nazis regarded his family as Jewish and that he was in danger of arrest. The Danish resistance helped him reach Sweden by sea, and he persuaded King Gustaf V to make public Sweden's willingness to give asylum to Jewish refugees. Historians disagree on how far this led to the rescue of over 7,000 Danish Jews. He joined the British Tube Alloys project and was part of the British mission to the Manhattan Project.
After the war Bohr called for international cooperation on nuclear energy and helped to establish CERN. He died on 18 November 1962, and the element bohrium is named after him.
niger-river: The Niger is the main river of West Africa, about 4,180 kilometres long, with a drainage basin of 2,117,700 square kilometres. It rises in the Guinea Highlands near the Sierra Leone border, only 240 km from the Atlantic, yet runs directly away from the sea into the Sahara. Near Timbuktu it turns sharply southeast and flows through Niger and Nigeria into the Gulf of Guinea. This boomerang course baffled geographers for two centuries; it apparently arose because two ancient rivers joined, the lower capturing the upper. Between Ségou and Timbuktu lies the Inner Niger Delta, braided streams, marshes and lakes whose seasonal floods make the land productive for fishing and agriculture.

When the African humid period ended some 5,500 years ago and the Sahara dried, people moved to the fertile Niger bend. Yams, African rice and pearl millet were domesticated in the region, and farming, fishing and herding led to settlements such as Djenné-Djenno, now a World Heritage Site. The bend became an origin and destination of trans-Saharan trade, which fuelled the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires, and ports such as Timbuktu and Gao became centres of learning. Gold, salt, kola nuts, fish, livestock, textiles and slaves moved along the river. Trade brought Islam to the region in approximately the 14th century.

Pliny connected the river to the Nile, and the notion persisted into the 19th century, even through the accounts of Leo Africanus, who first used the name Niger for it in 1550, and Ibn Battuta. The African Association was formed in England in 1788 to find the river. In June 1796 the Scottish explorer Mungo Park became the first European to see its middle part, and he died in 1806 on a second expedition. In 1830 Richard Lander and his brother were the first Europeans to follow the river to the ocean. The modern states of Niger and Nigeria take their names from it.

The river flows through Guinea, Mali, Niger, Benin and Nigeria, and its basin covers ten countries. Its main tributary, the Benue, joins it at Lokoja. Dams serve hydropower and irrigation, among them the Sélingué, Markala, Kainji, Shiroro and Jebba dams. The Inner Niger Delta covers about 20,000 square kilometres in the wet season and 3,900 in the dry, and supports migratory birds, fishing, farming and herding.
nigeria: Nigeria lies in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, between the Sahel to the north and the Atlantic Ocean to the south. It borders Niger, Chad, Cameroon and Benin. The Niger and Benue rivers converge in a Y shape and empty into the Niger Delta, one of the world's largest river deltas. The highest point is Chappal Waddi, at 2,419 metres.

The far south has a tropical rainforest climate, with mangrove swamps along the coast. Between the far south and the far north lies savannah, which divides into Guinean forest-savanna mosaic, Sudan savannah and Sahel savannah.

The Nok civilisation thrived between 1500 BCE and 200 CE. It produced life-sized terracotta figures that are among the earliest known sculptures in Africa, and it independently invented iron smelting by about 550 BCE and possibly a few centuries earlier. The Kano Chronicle records the history of the Hausa city state of Kano from around 999 CE, and other Hausa cities such as Daura, Katsina and Gobir have recorded histories dating to the 10th century.

The Kingdom of Nri of the Igbo people consolidated in the 10th century and lasted until it lost sovereignty to the British in 1911, and the oldest bronzes in West Africa made by the lost-wax process come from Igbo-Ukwu, a city under Nri influence. The Yoruba had developed one of the earliest city-states in Africa at Ile Ife by the 8th century. The Kingdom of Benin, founded by the Edo people, had a densely populated capital that served as a hub for regional and transatlantic trade in cloth, ivory, pepper and salt.

The name Nigeria was coined on 8 January 1897 by the British journalist Flora Shaw, after the Niger River. The modern state took its present shape in 1914 with the merging of the Southern Nigeria Protectorate and the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. Independence as a federation came on 1 October 1960, followed by a civil war from 1967 to 1970, a series of military governments, and civilian rule from 1999.

Nigeria is a federal republic of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with a bicameral National Assembly. More than 250 ethnic groups live there, speaking about 500 languages, and the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo together make up over 60% of the population.
nikita-khrushchev: Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev was born on 15 April 1894 in the village of Kalinovka, in the Kursk Governorate of the Russian Empire, to poor peasant parents. His father worked in the Donbas, where wages were much higher, and left the family in Kalinovka between visits. Khrushchev worked as a metal worker in his youth and was a political commissar in the Russian Civil War. In 1921 he was made assistant director for political affairs at the Rutchenkovo mine in the Donbas, and he had only four years of formal schooling.

Under the patronage of Lazar Kaganovich, who became head of the Party in Ukraine in 1925, Khrushchev rose quickly through the Soviet hierarchy. He expressed vehement support for the Moscow Trials of the Great Purge, and in 1938 he was sent to govern the Ukrainian SSR, where he continued the purges. In the Second World War he served as a political commissar and as an intermediary between Stalin and his commanders, and he was present at the Battle of Stalingrad.

Recalled to Moscow, he headed the Party in Moscow city and province from December 1949. After Stalin's death on 6 March 1953 a power struggle followed, in which Khrushchev prevailed over rivals including Lavrentiy Beria and was elected First Secretary of the Central Committee. On 25 February 1956 he delivered the Secret Speech at the 20th Party Congress, which denounced Stalin's purges and brought a less repressive era. His domestic policies, particularly in agriculture, were often ineffective. His years in office saw the tensest period of the Cold War, culminating in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.

Early in the 1960s his hold on power weakened because of his domestic failures and his handling of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Leonid Brezhnev began plotting his removal in March 1964, and he was ousted on 14 October 1964. He received a pension and a house, fell into deep depression, and was treated as a non-person. His memoirs were smuggled to the West and published in part in 1970.

Khrushchev died of a heart attack on 11 September 1971, aged 77. He was denied a state funeral and was buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow, with troops surrounding it. Many of his innovations were reversed after his fall. The historian Robert Service describes him as at once a Stalinist and an anti-Stalinist, a trouble-maker and a peacemaker.
nile: The Nile is 7,088 km long and flows north through north-east Africa into the Mediterranean Sea. The White Nile, the longer tributary, begins near Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile begins near Lake Tana in Ethiopia and contributes over twice the water volume of the White Nile. They meet at Khartoum, and the river then flows through the Nubian Desert to Cairo and empties near Alexandria into a large delta. The Blue Nile floods between July and October because of summer monsoon rains. The Nile has followed its present course for about 15,000 years.

When the climate of the eastern Sahara became drier around 3,900 BCE, herding peoples had to migrate to the Nile valley to survive, which was the origin of the Nubian cultures and of Ancient Egyptian civilization. The annual flood deposited silt along the banks and supported crops in the desert, though droughts that caused crop failures also brought famine. Irrigation, flood prediction and taxation called for new mathematical and administrative skills. South of the second cataract lay Nubia, home of the Kerma culture and the Kushite Empire. European explorations around Lake Victoria in the late 19th century located the river's source.

After British rule of Egypt began in 1882, the Aswan Low Dam was completed in 1902. Egypt and Sudan divided the river's flow by agreements of 1929 and 1959, and Egypt completed the Aswan High Dam in 1970. The basin spans eleven countries.
niue: Niue lies in a triangle drawn between Tonga, Samoa and the Cook Islands, about 2,400 kilometres north-east of New Zealand and 604 kilometres north-east of Tonga. It has a land area of about 261.46 square kilometres and is nicknamed The Rock, from its traditional name, the Rock of Polynesia. The terrain has two levels: a limestone cliff along the coast with a central plateau about 60 metres above sea level, and a coastal terrace about 500 metres wide. A coral reef surrounds the island, with its only major break on the central west coast, near the capital, Alofi. The wet season runs from November to April and the dry season from May to October.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Polynesians from Samoa settled Niue around 900 CE. According to Niuean tradition, further settlers came from Tonga in the 16th century as a war party. Until the beginning of the 18th century the island seems to have had no national government or single leader, and chiefs and heads of families held authority over parts of the population. A succession of patu-iki, or kings, then ruled, beginning with Puni-mata. Tui-toga, who reigned from 1875 to 1887, was the first of them to adopt Christianity.

The next documented European visitors represented the London Missionary Society. After many years of trying to land a European missionary, they abducted a Niuean named Nukai Peniamina and trained him as a pastor at the Malua Theological College in Samoa. He returned in 1846 and, after attempts in other villages had failed, was allowed to land at Mutalau, whose chiefs protected him day and night at the fort in Fupiu.

In 1889 the chiefs of Niue wrote to Queen Victoria asking her to stretch out your mighty hand, that Niue may hide herself in it and be safe, and expressed anxiety that another nation might take the island; the British did not at first take up the offer. A petition by Cook Islanders in 1900 asking for annexation included Niue if possible. The New Zealand Parliament restored self-government in 1974 with the Niue Constitution Act, after a referendum in which Niueans chose among independence, self-government and continuation as a New Zealand territory; the majority chose self-government. Robert Rex was elected by the Niue Assembly as the first Premier in 1974 and held the post until his death 18 years later.

Niue is a self-governing island country in free association with New Zealand, and its people are citizens of New Zealand. It is a parliamentary democracy divided into 14 villages, each sending a member to the Niue Assembly. Niue is bilingual, with Niuean and English spoken, and a large majority of Niueans live in New Zealand.
nizhny-novgorod: Nizhny Novgorod stands at the confluence of the Oka and the Volga in central Russia, 420 km east of Moscow. The Oka divides it into two parts: the Upper City on the hilly right bank, which includes the Kremlin, the historical and administrative centre, and the Lower City on the low western side, built up around the Gorky Automobile Plant. Originally the name was just Novgorod, meaning Newtown. To tell it from the older Novgorod to the west, it was called Novgorod of the Lower Lands, lower because it lay downstream of cities such as Moscow, Vladimir and Murom.

The city began as a small wooden hillfort founded by Grand Prince Yuri II of Vladimir in 1221 at the confluence of two of the most important rivers of his principality. It was the easternmost Russian settlement until 1372. After its incorporation into the Grand Principality of Moscow in 1392, the local princes took the name Shuysky and settled in Moscow. The Crimean Tatar chief Edigu burned the city in 1408; it was restored and regarded by the Muscovites as a great stronghold against the Tatars of Kazan.

The red-brick Kremlin, built in 1508-1511 under Pietro Francesco, withstood Tatar sieges in 1520 and 1536. In 1612 Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky organised an army in the city for the liberation of Moscow from the Poles and Lithuanians.

In 1817 the Makaryev Fair was transferred to Nizhny Novgorod and began to draw millions of visitors a year, so that by the middle of the 19th century the city was the trade capital of the Russian Empire. At the All-Russia exhibition of 1896, Alexander Popov's radio receiver and Vladimir Shukhov's hyperboloid tower were demonstrated. In the Soviet period the city became an important industrial centre, known as Gorky and nicknamed the Russian Detroit after the Gorky Automobile Plant. Shortly before the dissolution of the Soviet Union it took the name Nizhny Novgorod again.

Nizhny Novgorod is the administrative centre and largest city of Nizhny Novgorod Oblast and of the Volga Federal District, with about 1.2 million residents at the 2021 census. Its metro opened in 1985, and the city marked its 800th anniversary on 21 August 2021.
nobel-peace-prize: Alfred Nobel died in 1896 and left no explanation for adding a peace prize. According to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, his friendship with the peace activist Bertha von Suttner, herself later a recipient, profoundly influenced the decision. Some Nobel scholars suggest it was his way of compensating for developing destructive forces: his inventions included dynamite and ballistite, and he helped turn Bofors into an armaments company.

A well-known story that a French newspaper printed a premature obituary in 1888 calling him the merchant of death is reportedly apocryphal. His will says the prize goes to whoever has done the most or the best work for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies and for the holding and promotion of peace congresses.

The Norwegian Parliament appoints the five-member Norwegian Nobel Committee, which chooses the laureate. Each year the committee invites qualified people to nominate, among them members of national assemblies and governments, certain university professors and previous laureates. The statutes bar publication of information about nominations for 50 years, so the label 'Nobel Peace Prize nominee' has no official standing; in 1939 a Swedish parliamentarian made a satirical nomination of Adolf Hitler, mocking a serious one of Neville Chamberlain.

The prize is presented on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death, in the presence of the King of Norway, and is the only Nobel Prize not presented in Stockholm. The 1901 prize was 150,782 Swedish kronor. The medal, designed by Gustav Vigeland, shows three men in a fraternal bond.

The International Committee of the Red Cross has won three times, in 1917, 1944 and 1963, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees twice, in 1954 and 1981. Lê Đức Thọ is the only person to have declined the prize. The 1973 award to Henry Kissinger and Lê Đức Thọ may have been the most disputed: two members of the selection committee resigned in protest.

Mahatma Gandhi was nominated in 1937, 1938, 1939, 1947 and just days before his assassination in January 1948, but never won; in 1948 the committee made no award, on the grounds that there was no suitable living candidate. When the Dalai Lama received the prize in 1989, the chairman called it in part a tribute to Gandhi's memory.
nobel-prize: Alfred Nobel was born on 21 October 1833 in Stockholm into a family of engineers. He was a chemist, engineer and inventor who amassed a fortune from 355 inventions, dynamite among them. In 1894 he purchased the Bofors iron and steel mill, which he made into a major armaments manufacturer. A popular story holds that in 1888 he read his own obituary, titled The Merchant of Death Is Dead, in a French newspaper, when it was in fact his brother Ludvig who had died, and that this inspired him to change his will. Historians have been unable to verify the story, and some dismiss it as a myth.

Nobel died on 10 December 1896 in his villa in San Remo, Italy, of a cerebral haemorrhage, aged 63. His last will was signed in Paris on 27 November 1895. To widespread astonishment it specified that his fortune be used for prizes to those who confer the most benefit on mankind in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. He left 94 per cent of his assets, 31 million SEK, to establish the five prizes. Because of scepticism about the will, the Storting in Norway did not approve it until 26 April 1897, and its executors, Ragnar Sohlman and Rudolf Lilljequist, formed the Nobel Foundation.

The prizes were first awarded in 1901. A sixth prize, in Economic Sciences, was established in 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank in memory of Alfred Nobel and has been awarded since 1969. Except in special circumstances such as war, all are given annually. Each laureate receives a medal, a diploma and a monetary award. No more than three individuals may share a prize, though the Peace Prize can go to organisations. Prizes are not awarded posthumously, but one is presented if its winner dies after being named.

The process is similar for all prizes. Nomination forms go to about 3,000 individuals, generally prominent academics, with the deadline on 31 January. The committee nominates about 300 potential laureates, and nominees are not named publicly or told, and all nomination records are sealed for 50 years.

Four institutions choose the laureates by majority vote, and their decision cannot be appealed: the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for chemistry, physics and economics, the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute for physiology or medicine, the Swedish Academy for literature and the Norwegian Nobel Committee for peace. Winners are announced during the first two weeks of October.
norfolk-island: Norfolk Island lies in the Pacific Ocean between New Zealand and New Caledonia, 1,412 kilometres directly east of Australia's Evans Head and about 900 kilometres from Lord Howe Island. It covers about 35 square kilometres, with 32 kilometres of coast and no large internal bodies of water. Together with the neighbouring Phillip Island and Nepean Island it forms the Territory of Norfolk Island. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and mild, rainy winters. The evergreen Norfolk Island pine is native to the island and appears on its flag.

Archaeological investigation suggests that East Polynesian seafarers settled the island in the 13th or 14th century, either from the Kermadec Islands or from the North Island of New Zealand. Both Polynesian and Melanesian artefacts have been found. Occupation had ceased at least a few hundred years before Europeans arrived, probably because the island was isolated and poor for horticulture. Captain James Cook, on his second voyage, was the first European known to have landed, on 10 October 1774, and named it after Mary Howard, Duchess of Norfolk.

The island served as a convict settlement from 6 March 1788 until 5 May 1855, except for an interval between 15 February 1814 and 6 June 1825, when it lay abandoned. In 1824 the British government instructed the Governor of New South Wales, Thomas Brisbane, to reoccupy it as a place for what it called the worst description of convicts. The landing of 6 June 1825 brought 104 people, of whom 57 were convicts.

On 8 June 1856 permanent civilian settlement began, when 194 descendants of Tahitians and of the HMS Bounty mutineers, including those of Fletcher Christian, arrived from the Pitcairn Islands, which had become too small for their growing number. They occupied many of the buildings left by the penal settlements and established farming and whaling. Some families returned to Pitcairn in 1858 and 1863. Norfolk Island was part of New South Wales from 1788 to 1844, then of Van Diemen's Land, and was transferred from the United Kingdom to Australia in 1914.

Norfolk Island is an external territory of Australia, with its capital at Kingston and its largest town at Burnt Pine. The 2021 census counted 2,188 inhabitants. About half of the islanders trace their roots to Pitcairn Island. English and a creole called Norfuk, a blend of 18th-century English and Tahitian based on Pitkern, are both spoken. Tahitian influence survives in the hula dance and in dishes such as mudda, green banana dumplings. Tourism is the main economic activity.
norodom-of-cambodia: Norodom was born Ang Voddey on 3 February 1834, the eldest son of King Ang Duong, whom a peace treaty between Siam and Vietnam had recognised as king after decades of war fought largely on Cambodian soil. In 1850 his father sent him and his half-brother Prince Sisowath to study in Bangkok, where they grew up near members of the Siamese royal family. In 1857 he served in the Royal Siamese Army as a military adviser. He was elected to the throne in 1860.

In 1861 another half-brother, Si Votha, rebelled, and Norodom abandoned the capital of Oudong and fled to Bangkok. The Siamese court returned him to Phnom Penh early in 1862. He could not be crowned, because Siam held the royal regalia, which a Khmer monarch needed to be a legitimate ruler. After French military pressure, including a steamboat sent up the Chao Phraya river to Bangkok, the Siamese reluctantly gave the regalia back, and it was the French who crowned him in 1864.

The treaty of 1863 gave France control of Cambodia's foreign relations in exchange for his personal protection against his enemies. On 17 June 1884, with French gunboats anchored outside the Royal Palace, he was forced to sign a treaty giving up control of public revenue, customs taxes and public works. The anger this caused led in 1885 to a revolt against French rule under Si Votha; the French suspected Norodom of supporting it in secret. It ended when he assured Cambodians that the French had offered him concessions, and for a time afterwards the French were less inclined to press him. In October 1887 Cambodia became part of French Indochina.

He reduced the number of provinces to cut administrative costs and, following King Chulalongkorn of Siam, abolished commercial monopolies, slavery and the civil lists of the royal family. Under his supervision Wat Oudong was consecrated on 6 June 1875 and the Silver Pagoda built in 1892. Classical dance recovered prestige at his court, and after a visit to Manila in 1872 he brought Filipino musicians to Cambodia to teach modern music.

Norodom named his son Prince Norodom Yukanthor heir apparent, but Yukanthor fell out with the French and did not succeed. The king died in the palace at Phnom Penh on 24 April 1904 and was cremated in the traditional Buddhist fashion in 1906; his half-brother Sisowath followed him on the throne. His reign of 43 years and 188 days is the longest in Cambodian history that can be dated exactly.
north-africa: There is no single accepted scope for North Africa. The most common definition includes Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia and Western Sahara, while the United Nations also counts Sudan. Its southern boundary is sometimes placed at the Sahel, south of the Sahara.

The region has three main geographic features: the Sahara in the south, the Atlas Mountains in the west, and the Nile and its delta in the east. The Sahara covers more than 75 percent of the region. Fertile farmland lies in the sheltered valleys of the Atlas, in the Nile Valley and Delta, and along the Mediterranean coast, where olives, figs, dates and citrus fruits grow.

Finds at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco contain some of the oldest Homo sapiens remains known. The cave paintings of Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria depict daily life in the Neolithic Subpluvial period, about 8000 to 4000 BCE, before the Sahara dried rapidly around 3500 BCE. The northwest has been inhabited by Berbers since the beginning of recorded history, and the east was the home of the Ancient Egyptians and Nubians.

Phoenician and Greek colonies were founded on the coast in the 7th century BCE. Carthage, a Phoenician foundation, built a commercial empire, and its North African territories became the Roman province of Africa in 146 BCE. The kingdom of Mauretania was annexed by Emperor Claudius in 42 CE. In the early fifth century the Vandals crossed the Strait of Gibraltar, and the loss of Africa, an important grain province, weakened the Western Roman Empire.

The early Muslim conquests reached North Africa by 640, and by 700 most of it was under Muslim rule. Arab migrations followed, among them the westward movement of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym in the eleventh century, which historians regard as a critical moment in the Arabization of the countryside. Much of the area later came loosely under the Ottoman Empire, with the Barbary states on the coast. In the 19th century France, the United Kingdom, Spain and Italy brought the whole region under European occupation, and the North African states gained independence in the 1950s and 1960s.

Modern Standard Arabic is the official language of all the countries of North Africa, and Algeria and Morocco also recognize Berber as official. French serves as an administrative language in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia. The region is predominantly Muslim, with Jewish communities in Morocco and Tunisia and a significant Christian minority, the Copts, in Egypt.
north-america: North America is bordered to the north by the Arctic Ocean, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean, to the southeast by South America and the Caribbean Sea, and to the south and west by the Pacific Ocean. Its only land connection to South America is at the Darien Gap on the Colombia and Panama border. Some geologists place its southern limit instead at the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in Mexico. The Caribbean islands are considered part of it, and so is Greenland, which lies on the same tectonic plate. The Gulf of Mexico is the largest body of water indenting the continent, followed by Hudson Bay.

It is unknown exactly how and when the first human populations reached North America. People are known to have lived in the Americas at least 20,000 years ago, and some evidence points to earlier dates. The traditional theory is that hunters crossed the Bering Land Bridge between eastern Siberia and present-day Alaska; a growing view is that the first inhabitants sailed from Beringia some 13,000 years ago. Before European arrival the peoples of North America were divided into many polities, from small bands of a few families to large empires, and lived in cultural regions such as the bison-hunting Great Plains and farming Mesoamerica.

Norse exploration and colonization began in the late 10th century, with several settlements in Greenland and at least one in Newfoundland. From 1492 the voyages of Christopher Columbus began a transatlantic exchange, including migrations of European settlers. Present-day patterns reflect interactions among early European colonists, indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans and later immigrants from Europe and Asia. The Spanish Empire called its American territories Las Indias and governed them through a body named the Council of the Indies.

The name America comes from Amerigo Vespucci, through the German cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann, who placed it on a world map in 1507. Most North Americans speak English, Spanish or French, and significant indigenous populations keep their pre-colonial cultural and linguistic traditions. The continent includes the subregions of Northern America and Middle America, and the term is sometimes used for Northern America alone.
north-korea: In the late 19th century Korea came under the influence of Japan, which had won the First Sino-Japanese War against Qing China and the Russo-Japanese War against the Russian Empire. Japan compelled Korea to become its protectorate in 1905 and formally annexed it in 1910. A period of forced assimilation followed, in which Korean language, culture and history were suppressed. It led to the March First Movement protests in 1919 and to resistance groups in exile, primarily in China.

In the 1930s Japan developed mines, hydro-electric dams and steel mills in northern Korea and neighbouring Manchuria, so that 65% of Korea's heavy industry but only 37% of its agriculture lay in the north. A Korean guerrilla movement emerged in the mountainous interior and in Manchuria, and one of its most prominent leaders was the Communist Kim Il Sung.

After the Japanese surrender in 1945 the peninsula was divided into two occupation zones along the 38th parallel, the Soviet Union holding the north and the United States the south. Negotiations on reunification failed. Kim Il Sung became chairman of the Provisional People's Committee of North Korea, established in February 1946. The South declared its statehood in May 1948, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea was established in the North on 9 September 1948, with Kim Il Sung as premier.

Shtykov and Kim lobbied Joseph Stalin to support a quick war against the South, and it began in 1950 as the Korean War. The Korean Armistice Agreement of 1953 brought a ceasefire and established the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Kim Il Sung consolidated power and promoted his philosophy of Juche as the state ideology. The loss of Eastern Bloc trading partners and natural disasters in the 1990s brought a famine from 1995 to 1998, which an estimated 240,000 to 420,000 North Koreans did not survive.

North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula, covering 120,540 square kilometres. About 80 percent of it is mountains and uplands, and the highest point is Paektu Mountain at 2,744 metres, a sacred place in Korean culture. Pyongyang is the capital and largest city. The Workers' Party of Korea is the sole ruling party and the state owns almost all means of production. The Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong and the Complex of Koguryo Tombs are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
north-macedonia: North Macedonia has an area of 25,436 square kilometres and borders Serbia, Kosovo, Bulgaria, Greece and Albania. It constitutes approximately the northern third of the larger geographical region of Macedonia. A central valley formed by the Vardar river defines the country, framed by mountain ranges; the tallest is Mount Korab in the Šar Mountains, at 2,764 metres. Lake Ohrid, Lake Prespa and Dojran Lake lie on the southern borders, and Ohrid is considered one of the oldest lakes in the world. The region is seismically active, and an earthquake in 1963 heavily damaged Skopje and killed over 1,000 people.

In antiquity most of the area corresponded to Paeonia, a kingdom immediately north of ancient Macedonia, and Pelagonia. The Achaemenid Persians under Darius the Great conquered Paeonia in the late 6th century BCE and withdrew after 479 BCE. Philip II of Macedon absorbed Lynkestis, Pelagonia and the southern part of Paeonia into his kingdom in 356 BCE, and Paeonia became his vassal.

Rome conquered the region by the mid-2nd century BCE. Slavic tribes raided and settled it from the 6th century CE, and after contention between the Byzantine and Bulgarian empires it passed to the Serbian Empire in the mid-14th century and to the Ottoman Empire from the late 14th century.

The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 brought Serbian rule. Bulgaria ruled the territory during the First World War and again during the Second. After the Second World War it was established as a constituent state of communist Yugoslavia, and it seceded peacefully in 1991. The Socialist Republic of Macedonia had first adopted the name Macedonia officially at the end of the Second World War; the interwar Kingdom of Yugoslavia had prohibited its use.

The country took the name North Macedonia in 2019 under the Prespa Agreement. Many citizens still call it Macedonia. It joined the United Nations in 1993, has been a candidate for European Union membership since 2005 and is a member of NATO.

The 2021 census counted 1,836,713 people. The largest group is ethnic Macedonians, followed by Albanians, who dominate much of the north-west. Tensions over the balance of power between the two communities led to a brief war in 2001 and a power-sharing agreement. Macedonian is the official language, and Albanian is also co-official at state level.
north-ossetia-alania: The republic lies in the North Caucasus and covers about 8,000 square kilometres. Its northern part is on the Stavropol Plain, and about 22 per cent of its territory is forested. It borders Georgia, including South Ossetia, to the south, and Kabardino-Balkaria, Stavropol Krai, Chechnya and Ingushetia. Its highest point is Mount Kazbek, at 5,033 metres.

The region traces its history to the ancient Alans, who founded the Kingdom of Alania in the 8th century and adopted Christianity in the 9th. Alania profited from the Silk Road, which passed through its territory. In 1220 Genghis Khan sent his commanders Subutai and Jebe on a campaign that reached Alania, and in 1239 the Mongols destroyed its capital, Maghas, and other cities. The Alans were forced to flee to the mountain gorges and leave the flat lands. Islam was introduced in the 17th century by Kabardians.

Pressed by conflicts between the Khanate of Crimea and the Ottoman Empire, Ossetia entered an alliance with Russia in the 18th century, and Vladikavkaz became the first Russian-controlled area in the northern Caucasus. The Georgian Military Road was built in 1799, and by 1830 Ossetia was under complete Russian control. An estimated 50,000 Ossetians left the Caucasus in the early 1860s, as part of a wider migration of Muslims from the region to the Ottoman Empire. After 1917 North Ossetia was merged into the Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921, became an autonomous oblast on 7 July 1924 and an autonomous republic on 5 December 1936.

When the Soviet Union dissolved, the Ossetians were divided between North Ossetia, in the Russian republic, and South Ossetia, in the Georgian one. In 1992 a brief ethnic war between Ossetians and the Ingush took place in the Prigorodny District, and 30,000 to 60,000 Ingush were forced to leave North Ossetia. The name Alania, revived by Ossetian intellectuals in the last years of the Soviet Union, was added to the republic's title in November 1994.

The republic's capital is Vladikavkaz, at the foot of the Caucasus Mountains, and its population was 687,357 at the 2021 census. Ossetians form 68.1 per cent of it. Ossetian is an east Iranian language descended from the medieval Alanic and ancient Sarmatian languages. Most Ossetians are Eastern Orthodox Christians, and almost 30 per cent of the population follows the Ossetian ethnic religion, Uatsdin.
north-rhine-westphalia: North Rhine-Westphalia is a landlocked state in western Germany. It covers the plains of the Lower Rhine region and parts of the Central Uplands up to the gorge of Porta Westfalica, and it borders Belgium, the Netherlands, Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate and Hesse. The Rhine flows through it, and its banks are heavily populated and industrialised, particularly around Cologne and Düsseldorf. The state is not culturally uniform: customs differ significantly between the Rhineland and the regions of Westphalia and Lippe, and its flag combines their arms.

The first written account of the area is by Julius Caesar, who conquered the tribes on the left bank of the Rhine; the Eburones lived west of the river, and east of it he reported the Ubii and the Sugambri. Augustus established fortified posts on the Rhine, but the Romans never won a firm footing on the right bank. The Battle of Teutoburg Forest took place near Osnabrück, and Charlemagne is thought to have spent considerable time in Paderborn, with his Saxon Wars partly fought in Westphalia.

The British military administration established the state on 23 August 1946 by merging the Prussian province of Westphalia and the northern part of the Rhine Province. The former state of Lippe was added on 21 January 1947, and the state joined the Federal Republic in 1949. Bonn served as federal capital until the reunification of Germany in 1990 and as seat of government until 1999. A coal crisis began in 1958 and a steel crisis around 1967, ending the era in which the state was known as the land of coal and steel.

North Rhine-Westphalia has more than 18 million inhabitants and is the most populous German state. Düsseldorf is the capital and Cologne the largest city. Aachen Cathedral, Cologne Cathedral, the Zeche Zollverein in Essen, the Augustusburg Palace in Brühl and the Imperial Abbey of Corvey are World Heritage Sites. The University of Cologne, founded in 1388, is the oldest of its universities, and Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770.
north-sea: The North Sea lies on the European continental shelf and connects to the Atlantic Ocean through the English Channel in the south and the Norwegian Sea in the north. It is more than 970 kilometres long and 580 kilometres wide, covering 570,000 square kilometres, and has a mean depth of 90 metres; only the Norwegian trench, up to 725 metres deep, is much deeper. In the east it reaches the Baltic Sea through the Skagerrak and Kattegat.

Its coasts were shaped by glaciers: deep fjords in Norway and cliffs in Scotland in the north, and sandy beaches, estuaries and mudflats in the south. Its southern coasts were originally flood plains and swamp, and from about 1200 their people joined single ring dikes into a dike line along the coast.

There is little documentary evidence for the North Sea before the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 CE, but archaeology shows cultures and technologies spreading across it and some prehistoric peoples relying on fishing, whaling and seaborne trade. When the Romans left Britain in 410, the Angles, Frisians, Saxons and Jutes began the next great migration across the sea. It was the centre of the Vikings' rise, and the Hanseatic League, the Dutch Republic and Britain all later sought command of it. Flemish whalers worked the sea from the 9th until the 13th century, and were replaced in the 16th century by Dutch, English, Danes and Germans.

In the 17th century the Dutch Golden Age brought Dutch maritime power to its zenith, until England challenged it in the first three Anglo-Dutch Wars between 1652 and 1673, which ended in Dutch victories. After the Glorious Revolution of 1688 put the Dutch prince William on the English throne, power shifted from Amsterdam to London, and Britain faced no challenge in the North Sea until the 20th century.

In 1904 Russian ships on their way to the Far East fired on British fishing boats near the Dogger Bank, nearly bringing Britain into the Russo-Japanese War. As Germany's only outlet to the ocean, the sea was strategically important in both world wars.

The sea is bordered by Great Britain, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, and carries key north European shipping lanes. Offshore drilling began in 1966, and the Ekofisk field, found in 1969, began commercial production in 1971. The sea is Europe's main fishery, mostly by trawling. Until the First World War English also called it the German Ocean.
northern-mariana-islands: The Northern Mariana Islands are the 14 northern islands of the Mariana Archipelago, whose southernmost island, Guam, is a separate United States territory. Their area is about 475 square kilometres. The southern islands are limestone, with level terraces and fringing coral reefs, while the northern islands are volcanic, with active volcanoes on several, including Anatahan, Pagan and Agrihan. Mount Agrihan is the highest point, at 965 m. The climate is tropical rainforest, with a dry season from December to June and a rainy season, which can bring typhoons, from July to November.

The Mariana Islands were the first islands settled by humans in Remote Oceania, around 1500 to 1400 BCE, by people from the Philippines. Ferdinand Magellan, sailing under the Spanish flag, reached Guam in 1521 and claimed the archipelago for Spain, which made the islands part of the Spanish East Indies in 1565 and in the 18th century forced the people of the northern Marianas to relocate.

After the Spanish–American War, Spain ceded Guam to the United States and sold the rest of the Marianas to Germany under the German–Spanish Treaty of 1899. After the First World War they became part of the Japanese Mandate under the League of Nations. The Battle of Saipan in 1944 ended Japanese rule, and afterwards the islands were administered by the United States as part of the United Nations Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. In 1975 nearly 80% voted to become a commonwealth of the United States, and in 1977 over 93% approved the constitution of the commonwealth.

The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands is an unincorporated territory of the United States whose residents are United States citizens. The 2020 census counted 47,329 people, most of them on Saipan, Tinian and Rota, the only permanently populated islands. The administrative centre is Capitol Hill on Saipan. The northern islands were evacuated because of volcanic threat, and Pagan has been largely uninhabited since a 1981 eruption.
norway: Norway's core territory comprises the western and northernmost portion of the Scandinavian Peninsula, together with the island of Jan Mayen and the archipelago of Svalbard. Its total area is 385,207 square kilometres, or 323,808 without Svalbard and Jan Mayen. The rugged coastline is broken by huge fjords and thousands of islands, and the mainland coastline including fjords stretches 28,953 kilometres. Sognefjorden is the world's longest fjord at 204 kilometres. The Scandinavian Mountains form much of the border with Sweden, and about 400,000 lakes lie within the country.

The earliest traces of human occupation lie along the coast, where the ice shelf of the last ice age melted between 11,000 and 8000 BCE. The oldest finds are stone tools dating from 9500 to 6000 BCE, and between 3000 and 2500 BCE Indo-European farmers of the Corded Ware culture arrived in eastern Norway. Bronze was introduced around 1500 BCE, and the oldest known Norwegian runic inscription dates from the third century. By about the 8th century several small political entities existed, and it has been estimated that there were nine petty realms in Western Norway in the early Viking Age.

According to tradition, Harald Fairhair unified them into one kingdom in 872 after the Battle of Hafrsfjord, becoming the first king of a united Norway; according to the sagas, many Norwegians left the country to live in Iceland, the Faroe Islands, Greenland and parts of Britain and Ireland. From 1537 to 1814 Norway was part of Denmark–Norway, and from 1814 to 1905 it was in a personal union with Sweden. Its Constitution was adopted on 17 May 1814. Norway was neutral during the First World War, and was invaded and occupied by Nazi Germany from April 1940 until the end of the Second World War.

Norway has about 5.6 million inhabitants, with Oslo as its capital and largest city. It is a unitary constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system, and its unicameral Parliament, the Storting, has 169 representatives. The Sámi people are indigenous to the Far North, and the Sámi Parliament gives them a certain amount of self-determination. From the 19th century up to the 1970s the government tried to assimilate both the Sámi and the Kven through what is called the Norwegianization process.
nouakchott: Nouakchott lies in the southwest of Mauritania, on the Atlantic coast of the Sahara Desert, and is one of the largest cities in the Sahara. The ground is largely flat, and some of the city lies below sea level. Sand dunes advancing from the east pose a daily problem, and the coastal strip is mostly left empty and allowed to flood, apart from a small fishing port and the deepwater port. The city is built around the tree-lined Avenue Gamal Abdel Nasser, and other major streets are named for figures of the 1960s, among them Charles de Gaulle, Kennedy and Lumumba.

The site held a small fishing town, a fortified fishing village (ksar) in pre-colonial times and under French rule, inhabited by the Bouhoubainy, a tribe of Amazigh origin. Moktar Ould Daddah, the first President of Mauritania, and his advisers chose it because he wanted a capital that symbolised modernity and national unity, which ruled out the towns of the interior. It lay centrally between Saint-Louis in Senegal, from which the colony was governed, and Nouadhibou, and avoided the question of whether the capital stood in an area dominated by Arabs and Amazigh or by Sub-Saharan Africans.

The basics were completed by the time the French granted independence on 28 November 1960. The city was planned for 15,000 people, with broad streets in a grid and without the expectation that commerce would take place in it. The Polisario Front attacked it twice in 1976, causing little damage. From the 1970s drought and desertification drove hundreds of thousands to the city, many settling in overcrowded slums. It had only 20,000 people in 1969; censuses counted 134,000 in 1977 and 393,325 in 1988, probably below the reality, and 958,399 in 2013.

Nouakchott is the capital and largest city of Mauritania and the centre of its economy, with a deepwater port built by China that opened in 1986, an international airport and the University of Nouakchott, opened in 1981. It is divided into nine arrondissements and three regions, and holds the National Museum of Mauritania, the National Library and the National Archives. Most residents are Sunni Muslim, and it is a principal selling place of Saharan meteorites.
nova-scotia: Nova Scotia is a province on the east coast of Canada, in the Maritimes. It consists of the Nova Scotia peninsula, Cape Breton Island and some 3,800 other coastal islands, and is joined to the rest of Canada by the Isthmus of Chignecto, where its only land border, with New Brunswick, lies. Nowhere is more than 67 km from the ocean. The name is Latin for New Scotland, first given in the 1621 Royal Charter that granted Sir William Alexander the right to settle lands as a Scottish colony, including present Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and the Gaspé Peninsula.

The Mi'kmaq, of the Algonquian-language family, inhabited the land when Europeans arrived, as part of Mi'kma'ki, their territory across the Maritimes. In 1604 the French sailed into the Annapolis Basin but settled first at Saint Croix Island in Maine. In 1605 they founded Port Royal, which grew into Annapolis Royal: the first permanent European settlement in what later became Canada and the founding settlement of Acadia, France's first New France colony.

The Scots, English and then British fought France for the territory for over a century. Britain gained it in the Peace of Utrecht of 1713, which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, and Annapolis Royal remained the capital until Halifax was founded in 1749. The British then began settling foreign Protestants in the region and deported the French-speaking Acadians en masse. The Halifax Gazette, printed on 23 March 1752, was the first newspaper in Canada. Nova Scotia was ambivalent about joining the Americans, and thousands of Loyalists settled there during the American Revolutionary War.

In 1848 it became the first British colony to achieve responsible government. On 1 July 1867 the pro-Confederation premier Charles Tupper led it into Confederation with New Brunswick and the Province of Canada. The Anti-Confederation Party under Joseph Howe then won 18 of 19 federal seats and 36 of 38 provincial seats.

Nova Scotia is a Canadian province with a parliamentary system within a constitutional monarchy. Halifax is its capital and largest city, with over 45 per cent of the population at the 2021 census. It has the largest Scottish Gaelic-speaking community outside Scotland, and its Celtic music is kept alive each year at the Celtic Colours International Festival on Cape Breton Island.
novosibirsk: Novosibirsk stands on the banks of the Ob River in the West Siberian Plain, in the southwest of Siberia, about 2,811 kilometres from Moscow. Its southern boundary runs through the Novosibirsk reservoir, formed by the dam of the Novosibirsk Hydroelectric Station, which cuts through the Ob Plateau. The nearest major cities are Omsk, Barnaul, Kemerovo and Tomsk. The climate is typical of Siberia, with dry winters and temperatures far below freezing, since there is no ocean nearby and no tall mountains to the north to hold back the Arctic winds. It is the second-farthest substantially populated city from the ocean, after Ürümqi in China.

The Russian town began on 30 April 1893 on the right bank of the Ob, near an area traditionally inhabited by the Chat Tatars, at the future site of a Trans-Siberian Railway bridge. In 1895 it became known as Novonikolayevsk, in honour both of Saint Nicholas and of the reigning tsar, Nicholas II. It superseded the village of Bolshoye Krivoshchyokovo on the opposite bank, founded in 1696, which was resettled in 1893 because of the bridge. The bridge was completed in the spring of 1897 and made the settlement a regional transport hub. Its importance grew with the completion of the Turkestan-Siberia Railway in the early 20th century, which linked it directly with Central Asia and the Caspian Sea.

Before 1917 Novonikolayevsk had no traditional centre: the railway management buildings, the station, the chief cathedral and the city government were spread across the town. After the revolution Lenin House was built in 1925 on Krasny Prospekt, and the first Lenin monument stood near the station. The city was ravaged by the Russian Civil War but recovered in the early Soviet period and took its present name, Novosibirsk, in 1926. Work on the Opera House began in 1931 on the former market square, and under Stalin the city became one of the largest industrial centres of Siberia. After the outbreak of the Second World War it received many factories moved from the Russian core.

Novosibirsk is the administrative centre of Novosibirsk Oblast and the Siberian Federal District, and the third most populous city in Russia, with 1,633,595 people at the census of 2021. Its landmarks include the neo-Byzantine Alexander Nevsky Cathedral and the Novosibirsk Opera and Ballet Theatre, and Tolmachevo Airport is the busiest in Siberia. The metro, opened in 1985, was the first in Siberia.
nunavut: Nunavut covers 1,836,993.78 square kilometres of land and 160,930 square kilometres of water in Northern Canada. It includes a substantial part of the mainland, most of the Arctic Archipelago, and the waters and islands of Hudson Bay, James Bay and Ungava Bay, among them Ellesmere Island in the far north, parts of Victoria Island and the distant Belcher Islands and Akimiski Island. The highest point is Barbeau Peak, at 2,616 metres, on Ellesmere Island. Its boundary with the Northwest Territories roughly follows the tree line. Most regions have a polar climate, and the more southerly continental areas a very cold subarctic one.

The mainland was first populated about 4,500 years ago by the Pre-Dorset, a Paleo-Eskimo culture that moved east from the Bering Strait region, and the Dorset culture, which developed from it, followed about 2,800 years ago. The Thule people, ancestors of the modern Inuit, began to migrate from Alaska in the 11th century, and by 1300 their settlement covered most of modern Nunavut. They replaced the Dorset genetically and culturally after 1300. The earliest written account of the area dates from 1576, when the English explorer Martin Frobisher, seeking the Northwest Passage, made the first recorded European contact with the Inuit in what is now Frobisher Bay. Henry Hudson, William Baffin and Robert Bylot followed in the 17th century.

In the 1950s, as part of the High Arctic relocation, the federal government moved Inuit from Nunavik, in northern Quebec, to Resolute and Grise Fiord, where they faced starvation but were forced to stay. A 1994 report led to compensation. Debate on dividing the Northwest Territories along ethnic lines began in the 1950s, and a plebiscite on division was held on 14 April 1982. The land claims agreement was completed in September 1992 and ratified by nearly 85% of voters in Nunavut. Parliament passed the Nunavut Act and the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act on 9 July 1993, and the territory was established on 1 April 1999, the first major change to Canada's political map since Newfoundland joined in 1949.

Nunavut's capital is Iqaluit, on Baffin Island, chosen in a plebiscite in 1995. Other major communities are Rankin Inlet and Cambridge Bay. The 2021 census counted 36,858 people, of whom 84.3% identified as Inuit. The official languages are the Inuit language, Inuktut, which includes Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun, English and French. Alert, on Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost continuously inhabited place. Nunavut is Canada's only geopolitical region not connected to the rest of North America by the Pan-American Highway.
nuno-da-cunha: Born about 1487, Nuno da Cunha was the son of Antónia Pais and of Tristão da Cunha, the navigator, admiral and ambassador to Pope Leo X. He first proved himself in the fighting at Oja and Brava and at the capture of Panane, under the viceroy Francisco de Almeida. King John III of Portugal, to whom he had been close since the king was a prince, named him ninth governor of the Portuguese possessions in India, with orders to end the government of Lopo Vaz de Sampaio and send him to Portugal in chains.

The pirates he subdued at Mombasa on the passage out had been harassing the coast of Portuguese Mozambique, whose watering stations were essential to the route to western India. His brothers Pero Vaz da Cunha and Simão da Cunha were to have served as his second and third in command, as was expected in the Estado da Índia, but both died on the voyage, and during his long rule he had to rely on local networks of clientage in Goa. He took office in April 1529 and held it for nine years, longer than any other governor of Portuguese Asia in the sixteenth century.

In 1529 he sent an expedition that sacked and burned Damão in Gujarat. On 20 January 1533 forces under his control captured Baxay, the later Bassein and present Vasai, from Bahadur Shah. The next year it became the capital of the Portuguese province of the North, and its citadel of black basalt was begun; the citadel was completed in 1548 and still stands. In 1538 an army of the Sultanate of Gujarat under Khadjar Safar, aided by Ottoman forces, besieged the Portuguese in Diu.

Court intrigues forced his return to Portugal. He was shipwrecked at the Cape of Good Hope on the way and drowned; his death is dated 5 March 1539. He had married first Maria da Cunha and then Isabel da Silveira. The main source for his career is the history of the Portuguese in the East by João de Barros, who lived from 1496 to 1570.
nuremberg: Nuremberg is the largest city of the cultural region of Franconia and the second-largest city of Bavaria, on the Pegnitz river. It forms a continuous conurbation with Fürth, Erlangen and Schwabach. Its location on key trade routes, and later at the junction of railways, highways and the Rhine–Main–Danube Canal, shaped its rise as a commercial centre.

The first documentary mention of the city, in 1050, names it as the location of an imperial castle. King Conrad III established the Burgraviate of Nuremberg, and Frederick I of the House of Hohenzollern inherited it in 1193. The city became a Free Imperial City in the 13th century, imperial diets were frequently held there, and the Imperial Regalia were kept in the city from 1424 until the end of the empire. Its cultural flowering in the 15th and 16th centuries made it the centre of the German Renaissance; Albrecht Dürer, a native, produced the first printed star charts in 1515. It accepted the Reformation in 1525.

The Nazi Party chose the city as the site of its large conventions, the Nuremberg rallies, held in 1927, 1929 and annually from 1933 to 1938, with the Rally Grounds designed by Albert Speer. At the 1935 rally Hitler ordered the Reichstag to convene at Nuremberg to pass the Nuremberg Laws, which revoked German citizenship for all Jews and other non-Aryans. Between 1945 and 1946 an international tribunal tried German officials for war crimes and crimes against humanity there; the Soviet Union had wanted Berlin, but Nuremberg had symbolic value.

Nuremberg has 546,397 inhabitants (2024) and is a centre of transport, education and commerce in northern Bavaria. It is known for its well-preserved medieval heritage, including Nuremberg Castle, the Old Town and the city walls, much of it rebuilt after the Second World War. The Heilig-Geist-Spital, founded in 1332, stands on the Pegnitz, and its museums show the world's oldest globe, built in 1492. Gingerbread known as Lebkuchen and grilled sausages are its traditional foods.
nuuk: Nuuk stands at the mouth of the Nuup Kangerlua fjord on the south-western coast of Greenland, about 240 kilometres south of the Arctic Circle. At 64°11′ N it is the northernmost capital in the world, a few kilometres farther north than Reykjavík. The mountain Sermitsiaq, 1,210 metres high, can be seen from almost everywhere in the town. The climate is a maritime-influenced tundra, with long, cold, snowy winters and short, cold summers. Nuuk is the Greenlandic word for cape.

The Paleo-Eskimo Saqqaq culture lived in the area as far back as 2200 BCE, and Norse settlers lived there from about 1000 until their settlement disappeared, for uncertain reasons, in the 15th century.

The city proper began in 1728, when the royal governor Claus Paarss moved the missionary Hans Egede's Hope Colony, founded in 1721, to the mainland, at the Inuit settlement of Nûk. The fort was named Godt-Haab, good hope. Paarss's colonists were mutinous soldiers, convicts and prostitutes, and most died of scurvy and other ailments within the first year. A smallpox epidemic in 1733 and 1734 killed most of the native population as well as Egede's wife, and Egede returned to Denmark in 1736.

In 1733 Moravian missionaries received permission to found a mission, which became the nucleus of present-day Nuuk as many Greenlanders moved to it. In 1861 Hinrich Johannes Rink began Atuagagdliutit, Greenland's first newspaper, with a Greenlander as editor. The city grew rapidly in the 1950s, when Denmark began to modernise Greenland.

Nuuk is the capital and largest city of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, and the seat of its government, with 20,113 inhabitants, more than a third of the territory's population. The Greenland Home Rule government renamed Godthåb as Nuuk on 1 May 1979.
